Ok, so what is this game about? Well... (very mild spoiler)
You're a guy who plays a VR-MMORPG where PvP becomes a growing problem for new players.
After getting killed, you join a guild and have a good time with them, until you encounter a guy who kills your guild girlfriend, who falls into a coma right after that. You hunt that guy down, and he also kills you and fries your computer system.
You restart the computer, and everything's gone. Even your mails are gone, and your character is back to level 1.
You have no items and no clue what happened to your old friends. This is the point when the actual game starts.

Sounds like a lot? It was just a very small tutorial and a few cutscenes filling about the first 1-2 hours of the game.
If that's not your cup of tea, avoid this game and many other JRPG'ish games. You've been warned! ;-)

Now it's your job to level up again, meet new friends in a simulated MMORPG and search for clues about the mysterious guy who almost killed you and your comatose online girlfriend.
To do that, you form groups, visit randomized field and dungeon maps, and grind the hell out of the game. (MMORPG simulation, remember?)
The combat system is a mix of real-time and stopping the game to select actions like spell casting, using items, etc.

Well, and that's it. You play a simulated MMORPG that contains all the stuff MMORPGs are about. Inviting people to your party, exploring randomized areas, grinding for XP/Gold/Items and between doing this stuff, you read/watch a lot of story.
Between all the grinding, there's also a desktop to explore. Yes, you can "shut down the game" and return to your desktop, where you read mails, search forums, answer messages and read the local news. The real world has an ongoing story, and events happening inside the game may show some feedback in the games real world.

To be clear, this is not made for everybody. But if you can enjoy a good grind while exploring a deep and huge story filled with funny (sometimes annoying) characters in a world that just oozes MMORPG clichés, Welcome to The World!

(For more information, you should really check out the whole .hack// franchise. If you're not familiar with it, please give it a try. It was the SAO before the SAO and the Isekai before the Isekai. A very big and mysterious world full of crazy Super AI, life-threatening bugs and glitches, digital horror dimensions and lots more spread over anime, manga, novels and video games.)

The .hack//G.U. series is a great entry in the underrated .hack// multimedia franchise. It blends engaging storytelling with an innovative take on the MMORPG genre in a single-player format. Even though it was originally released years ago, this 2017 remake offers longtime fans and newcomers alike a chance to experience the complete G.U. saga in one package.

The collection includes all of the GU games, and it often goes on sale for ~$4.99 so I recommend picking it up during a price drop. Each game offers roughly 20 hours of gameplay if you explore everything, making it manageable for those who want a full experience without an overwhelming time investment.

What truly sets this series apart is its rich narrative, tackling themes of identity, technology, and human connection in the context of a fictional MMORPG called The World. It captures the intrigue of early-internet online gaming communities while weaving an emotional and thought-provoking story. I love that the game is a little "meta" since you have a desktop, emails, web forum, and the "game" itself to help build the story beyond what's happening in the MMORPG. It's also cool to read the "news" and see just how the developers in 2006-2007 hit the nail on the head with tech like this, in some ways.

This franchise deserves more recognition and a chance to shine with modern resources. Sadly I think it's been abandoned, but this entry is worth picking up during a sale.

Masterpiece of a series that's in dire need of attention from bandai namco to revive it. Played the original PS2 games as a child that now go for ridiculous prices online, and played this remaster day 1 on PS4 when it came out, putting in around 200 consecutive hours of playtime. My PS4 soon crashed and corrupted all my saves, but that's neither here nor there. Experiencing the story in the year it was set in (2017) was a very surreal and unique experience I'll never forget.

The graphics and amazing cutscenes CC2's known for hold up to and even surpass games releasing in the current year. The characters in .hack are some of the most realistic depictions of humans I've seen in any fiction, right down to the most mundane everyday scenarios and character interactions. Also, this game very accurately predicted where technological advancement would be in the year it's set in. 

The writing is meta and self-aware, and the series perfectly exhibits the true mmo experience. This series is very much a product of its time that captures that time perfectly. Browsing the forums really immerses you in the feeling of playing and interacting with other people, while also adding many subplots.

Hopefully soon .hack IMOQ will finally be remastered as well... Playing these games always invokes both a sense of nostalgia and a yearning for future installments to continue one of, if not my favorite series of all time.

.Hack//SIGN was the first anime I got SERIOUSLY into back before the before times. Then I followed it up with the first 4 games after the series ended. Then I found and watched .Hack//ROOTS (and the other quirky bracelet spin-off, but that one was kind of weird).

Then I see it's 85% off? 8 bucks? I spend that much on breakfast some times! Why wouldn't I buy it?

Anyway, the old world-building ways are back. Lots and LOTS of reading. I think in the first two and a half hours I've put into the game, maybe 15 minutes of it were playing through the tutorial.

Then you get CTDed (not ACTUALLY a CTD, but an In Game CTD) and there's just READING and READING and READING.
I'm one of these people who gets twitchy if I see a 'NEW!' tag on an element, so I have to go through and clear everything until there are no more new tags.

But it was also interesting, and a neat way to sort of immerse the player into the world that exists between the real world, where you are now, reading this weird review, and the one in the video game. You know, 'ZA WARULDO!' There's a lot of lore and stuff in those news articles and 'forum posts' that I imagine people familiar with the story of the entire .Hack//CANON will read and start to wonder 'Okay, so... what the f*** is gonna happen when $#!+ gets f***y with all of this stuff they're talking about?'

I know I am.

It's not a game for someone who isn't invested in the series yet. The dialogue is poorly written and edited, but the voice actors are great. Liam O'Brien, Sam Riegel and Yuri Lowenthal are some standouts. I think that the dated look of the game also takes a bit of investment to look past. And it is decidedly geared towards an Eastern audience, with jokes, gags and philosophies that don't translate well to an English adaptation.

That said, as a long-time fan of the .Hack franchise, I can't let anyone who loves the series pass this by without at least a second glance. I recommend it to everyone who watched //Roots, and if you haven't, I would say you should before playing through the G.U. games.

Not much to say other than "This game is amazing!". Great story, great gameplay, awesome character development and a whole bunch of other things that make it a solid 10/10 experience! Worth every penny!

The biggest flaw is one early section where the cutscenes drag on too long, but even then one has to appreciate the consistent quality of voiced dialogue and of the animated cutscenes. What would have been shocking story-production values for any game back then are not outstanding now, but the animations remain cool, and the overall feeling in G.U. is that of watching an early 2000's anime. Though combat is shallow throughout Volume 1, and easily mastered, it feels satisfying (especially counterattacks) and is enough to break up the plot. The addition of a second weapon and PvP battles add life to Vol.1 at just the right time, and any disappointment with the slow-to-develop combat system is balanced by surprisingly good features of other kinds.

This is a story game akin to a visual novel, with a text burden exceeding most other story-focused RPGs. if you don't like to read, you'll miss out on elements that give the setting depth and build expectations. G.U. has an email system, and is full of forum posts and other media elements that simulate the MMO community, as well as news articles which release over the course of the main story. Not only do forum threads contain tips and 'map coordinates' that can be used inside the game, the 'players' talk variously about the effects of technology on human social interactions, the dangers of surveillance, and other issues that are ever more relevant today. The themes are strong, and add reality to the setting despite that the main story does not get especially deep within the first 20 hours ('Volume 1').

Various gameplay elements also add to to the vividly realised MMO atmosphere. The best way to get expensive items is to trade with 'players' (NPCs) found wandering the hub world, and offload extra copies of rare items you've acquired for new ones that you lack. There are quests, a guild rank system, and every player character has a class, which tells you their abilities in the PvP encounters. New weapons and abilities came too slowly, but the great atmosphere and gameplay variety help one forgive that the combat has not aged especially well - it's on about the level of an old Tales game.

If you can tolerate the occasional sluggish, tropey anime scene near the beginning, you will find that character development and important plot events happen densely and continuously. With the exception of the Canard members' introduction - a short arc that takes too long and kills the pace for a couple hours just after the blazing intro - the pacing is good. The expressive voice acting is awesome, but means you will be unable to speed through textboxes as in other RPGs, so you must either wait or skip the scene entirely. But it is a rare scene where nothing interesting is happening. Overall, faster-paced scenes with special animations are abundant and the character writing is pretty good(!). Haseo's experiences have believable and often relatable effects on his worldview, and change how he interacts with others: he struggles not to come to extreme conclusions, and his allies have noticeable effects on his personality more often than not.

At time of writing I'm just entering Vol.2, and things are continuously getting more exciting. I wonder what the story will say in the end about the intertwining of physical and digital realities and the resulting effects on people. Here is a compelling mystery about a disaster-prone company developing the MMO, secret game glitches, and the effects of unintended game events on the real players behind the characters. It's like a book that I wish I could read a little faster.

.hack//G.U. Last Recode is a thoughtfully remastered collection that brings together the acclaimed trilogy of action RPGs from the early 2000s, delivering an immersive dive into the cyber-themed universe of “The World.” For fans of narrative-driven games and those interested in the early roots of online RPG storytelling, this collection offers a rich, layered experience that combines a compelling story with engaging combat and intricate character development. The remaster does a solid job of modernizing visuals and controls, making the classic title more accessible to new players while still preserving the atmosphere that longtime fans cherish.

The narrative is at the heart of Last Recode, continuing the tradition of deep, character-focused storytelling that the original series was known for. Players step into the shoes of Haseo, a determined and somewhat brooding protagonist on a quest to uncover the truth behind mysterious in-game events and his own tragic past. The game blends themes of friendship, identity, and the blurred lines between virtual and real worlds, weaving a story that unfolds across three distinct but interconnected episodes. The layered plot is compelling, with well-written dialogue and memorable character arcs that keep players invested throughout the lengthy campaign.

Gameplay strikes a balance between traditional JRPG mechanics and more dynamic, action-oriented combat. The real-time battles are fluid and satisfying, requiring players to strategize using a combination of attacks, skills, and tactical positioning. The game introduces a unique “Avatar” system, allowing Haseo to switch between different fighting styles, which adds variety and depth to encounters. Character progression is robust, with skill trees and equipment upgrades that encourage experimentation and personalization. While some may find the combat less fast-paced than modern action RPGs, it maintains a rhythm that rewards both timing and tactical thinking.

Visually, Last Recode benefits greatly from its remaster. The updated character models, refined textures, and improved lighting effects bring the world of “The World” to life in vibrant detail. While the core art style retains its early 2000s charm, the enhancements make the environments more immersive and the character animations smoother. The soundtrack, a blend of atmospheric and energetic tracks, complements the cyberpunk setting perfectly, enhancing both tense battles and quieter narrative moments. Voice acting is generally strong, helping to deepen emotional connections to the story and characters.

One of the more impressive aspects of Last Recode is how it respects and expands the original trilogy’s content. In addition to the main story episodes, the remaster includes Rebirth, an additional chapter that wraps up lingering plot threads and provides closure to Haseo’s journey. This extra content is welcomed by fans who have followed the series, as it adds new layers to the story and gameplay without feeling tacked on. The collection also streamlines some quality-of-life improvements such as faster load times and better camera controls, addressing frustrations players had with the original releases.

Despite its strengths, the game does have moments where its age shows. Some pacing issues linger, especially during the exploration and dungeon segments, which can feel repetitive or overly drawn out. The narrative’s focus on anime-style storytelling and occasional melodrama might not appeal to everyone, and the reliance on text-heavy exposition can slow down the momentum for players used to more streamlined storytelling. However, these aspects are part of the series’ identity and may even be a draw for those who appreciate classic JRPG sensibilities.

In conclusion, .hack//G.U. Last Recode stands as a comprehensive and polished remaster that successfully introduces a classic JRPG trilogy to a modern audience. It combines a rich, emotionally engaging narrative with solid combat mechanics and updated visuals, delivering a nostalgic yet fresh experience. While it may not revolutionize the genre, it offers a meaningful journey for fans of story-driven games and cyberpunk aesthetics. For players interested in exploring the origins of narrative complexity in online RPGs or those seeking a thoughtful, character-driven adventure, Last Recode is a rewarding and memorable title.

I have mixed feelings for this game and wouldn't recommend it if I didn't get this game when it was heavily discounted(got it when it as around 17aud).

Lets start with the cons first. The game is piss easy. As long as you got to max level per volume which isn't hard or that time consuming at all. All the fights are pretty much a landslide for the player. The combat itself isn't bad, but the rengeki system for example limits how the player uses skills. In addition to the fixed cd after using skills/item/charge attack and later benefits for rengeki, there's no point to using skills beyond for rengeki. Comparing it similar style games like the Tales series, the pacing of the combat is fairly lackluster and, quite frankly, annoying at times. Minor things like QoL improvements are only unlocked late in the game which kinda beats the purpose and the avatar battle is quite boring and repetitive. The story has very obvious filler moments that makes you wonder why they're there other than to drag out another 10-15 minutes.

The good parts along with the discount I got made were able to overshadow the bad and allowed me to finish the game. The story is quite nice, as someone that did watch the original .Hack anime and the OVA trilogy, I might be a bit bias here, but overall, the story is pretty solid with compelling moments here and there. The forum/news/email part may get a bit annoying but it actually is a pretty smart mechanic/element of the game that helps the narration of the game and further sets the mood for the player. Of course due the language translation and cultural difference, there are weird parts here and there but the forums are surprising realistic in many ways, and the Online Jack section is actually quite interesting. The game also features some pretty good music here and there which I guess is the icing on the top.

In conclusion, if you like JRPG and can get it when it's on discount like I did during the summer sales, then this game isn't bad at all.

Notes:
- .Hack//G.U. Last Recode covers the G.U. portion of the .Hack series and what happened after .Hack//Roots, which is an 26-episode anime series (Optional but not required to understand the story past Volume 1). 

- The first 4 installments where Kite is the protagonist (.Hack//Infection and so on) are not included and are NOT required to understand the full story of G.U.

- Other than that, there's complementary content and alternate versions of G.U. outside of the game but this game is the canon story of the G.U. portion and other games, mangas and animes are vaguely referenced in the game as a jig and not part of the main story.

Main Story: The game starts where the .Hack//Roots left off after the Twilight Brigade events where Haseo becomes a PKK (Player-killer killer) and hunts for Tri-edge to avenge his friend Shino. The game is divided into 3 acts where Volume 4 serves as a 3-hour long Epilogue to the whole G.U. Saga. Online Jack (on the News Capture) occurs at the same time as the G.U. events.

Gameplay: It's a 2007 JRPG where you smash Attacks to perform 1-2-3 combos and use skills as a mix-up. Combos change depending on the weapon and you gain more weapon-types later in Volume 2, a slight rework in Volume 3 and a full rework in Volume 4. It's a 2007 game, it can feel severly dated yet nostalgic- very similar to Tales of Games.
You gain increased EXP from enemies with higher level, Damage scales off Level disparity, between the range 1 to 10 and grinding for EXP isn't much of a thing unless you skip pass all the enemies on the field- but it doesn't take long to find a word combination outside the main story and start grinding 3 - 5 levels in 10mins.

Exploration: You use a 3-word system to generate an instance and walk around hallways with enemies located on specific areas, repeating the same combination of words will yield the same result and you can fine tune the enemy's level range and rewards with the 2nd and 3rd word- as well as area objective and location. It can feel quite repetitive.

Aesthetic: The game tries to replicate the feel of booting up your old PS2, XB360 or even Gamecube menu with functions like email, movies, forums and such to emulate the feeling of an old PC from the early 2000s. Every time you logout the game, it's as if you're done for the day and log in the next day, hence the gimmick of "logout > check email > login > repeat" model through the entire game's story.

Rating: As dated as the game is, it's a solid 6/10 for new people, 7/10 for those who ride on the nostalgia of old games and probably a 7.5 to 8/10 for the .hack fans- as it's the last game CyberConnect released since 2017 related to the .hack series. 
If Bandai allowed them, they would, willingly, make a sequel, with all of these traits updated to today's design philosophies and a modern twist to the .hack series.

Nostalgia and Love for the Series put aside,

-Dungeon Crawler
-Friendship meter with Characters
-Some choice interactions(Basiclly good or bad choices)

A fundamental misunderstanding about this game is that is tagged as a "Story Rich - JRPG" - the thing is, this is not a JRPG, this a Visual Novel pretending to be a JRPG.
The reason for why it does this, is that the main character playing in an MMORPG is core to the story, and so to convey that and have you immerse better in this narrative, it needs for you to walk inside that MMORPG, however shallow and linear this representation of a MMORPG is. 
The gameplay being so linear, the "fields" being all identical randomly generated aggregation of few square rooms, the combat being so shallow and you so overpowered/overleveled all the time clearly hint to the fact this is not even trying to be a good JRPG, it needs that only as a background to tell the story of this Visual Novel.
Therefore is you, the player, that has to imagine that the MMORPG the Main Character is interacting with is far more rich, open world an immersive.

Ultimately, if you enjoy this game or not depends in which box/category you try to fit it in:
・if you consider this a JRPG, chances are you'll be disappointed by the lacking combat
・if you consider this a Visual Novel, the story is intriguing and it's quite enjoyable, I would say superior to other VN because it being 3D and animated, makes it feel like you're just watching an anime (with some interaction here and there, running from point A to B etc..)

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#503 out of 700+)... it's time for .hack//G.U. Last Recode.

In the great pantheon of classic PS2-era Japanese-style roleplaying games, the [i].hack[/i] series is perhaps among the most-fondly remembered and also—paradoxically—least-discussed. Boasting a unique (at the time) premise—people trapped inside of an MMO, where death or injury in the game equates death or injury in reality—and an ahead-of-its-time episodic release structure, the .hack series was an ambitious project that consistently failed to fully realize its own aspirations.

Much of your enjoyment in the G.U. trilogy is dependent on how inherently interesting you find the games' core premise, as well as how fondly you feel about the character (who mostly fill out the expected early-2000s [i]shounen[/i] anime archetypes. In other words, the combat isn't terribly impressive or engaging. In the first game, you can smash into enemies with one of two weapons (dual daggers or a greatsword) and each sequel adds on additional weapon you can use as well (a scythe and dual pistols, respectively). Each weapon has a handful of special techniques, and then there's the [i]rengeki[/i] special attack/counterattack options to make things a bit more dynamic. And as one would expect, most enemies are especially vulnerable or resistant to specific weapon types. Most of the difficulty arises from level disparities—if you want any kind of challenge, you'll only find it against enemies of significantly higher level than the player. Unfortunately, because this remaster rebalanced experience progression, you will most often be several levels above the foes in whatever area you find yourself in—especially if you spend any time at all completing sidequests. This ultimately reduces the game to a fairly mindless ARPG—I don't think I ever had to use even a single healing option. Even up against powerful optional bosses. This is one of those games where you'll hit the level cap about a dozen hours before finishing each game, which always feels pretty unsatisfying, yeah?

And then there's the story. You'd think there'd be a lot of fertile ground to explore with a premise like G.U.'s, but the narrative we wound up with is surprisingly unambitious and unimaginative. This is one of those cases where the writers have an interesting premise, yet remain totally disinterested in exploring it. The plot of all three games, for example, hinges on drawn out tournament sequences—while the more interesting aspects of the setting, viruses and artificial intelligence and other heady science fiction concepts are only ever referenced or alluded to, with no meaningful exploration or discussion. The end result is a story that, essentially, is no more than a [i]shounen[/i] tournament anime with some interesting SF set dressing.

All that said, despite the weak gameplay and disappointing storytelling, the .hack//G.U. trilogy is still solidly fun to play through, owing mostly to presentation. It is astonishing, frankly, how well the pre-rendered animation holds up (putting many—or most—modern games to shame, some twenty years later. The animation, too, is especially praiseworthy, featuring some truly fantastic and well-choreographed action sequences. All of which is set to the background of a delightfully baroque, steampunk world and a genuinely god-tier soundtrack. In all earnestness, and I cannot stress this enough, [b]the music is phenomenal; achingly beautiful[/b]. 

And while the ubiquitous “normal gampelay” environments are about as generic as they come, it's impossible not to appreciate how evocative the landscapes of the unique “lost grounds” are—many resembling the oft-praised designs of much later games, like [i]Bioshock[/i] and [i]Dark Souls.[/i]

The end result is that /hack//G.U. is a popcorn game—certainly sufficiently entertaining, but far from thought-provoking. And it's hard not to exit the series without feeling disappointed by its lack of imagination. This is a setting where the boundaries between simulated worlds and reality are blurred and muddy, each seeping over into the other—where electronic viruses can infect human souls and manipulate our emotions, and eventually become self-aware. All very interesting, potentially profound SF concepts used only as decoration. If, perhaps, the games' had some set of compelling ideas or themes to explore, this would be forgivable, but mostly the narrative just reeks of a story that had very little thought put into it—even by the end, even with the bonus fourth game included in this remaster, it's clear that none of the writers involved had a clear vision of what kind of story they wanted to tell. So they gesture at the SF concepts lightly while regurgitating the same tournament-style plot again and again. The contextual justification for the tournaments differs slightly from game to game, but ultimately you're stuck going through the same motions three times 'round.

You might think that in another, better world the new fourth game included here—really little more than an extended epilogue—would be an opportunity to finally dig in to the SF issues... but, once again, the writers swerve hard into tiresome tropes and refuse to do anything but the bare minimum. Presumably this apathy is a direct result of marketing concerns: I'm told that the peripheral .hack media does a better job exploring these ideas—but if so, they've sorely misjudged. If you want to get your audience interested enough in a story to consumer peripheral media, you do that by making the initial story interesting, not cutting those interesting bits out to sell piecemeal later.

Perhaps it may seem I'm being overly critical here, and perhaps I am—but it's hard to play through these games without wondering at how much more interesting they[i]very easily[/i] could have been. Even the conceit of playing an MMO, and being able to “exit” the game to the user's PC desktop is woefully unexplored. You'll occasionally read message board posts, but have no real ability to interact with anyone, and even the email chains rarely prompt replies. This has the (most likely) unintended affect of painting Haseo's real-life player as deeply antisocial: a person who spends much of their time lurking on message boards and reading emails, but unwilling or incapable of communicating with any other human beings outside of the very narrow context of the MMO setting. And, look, I get it (selective mutism sucks, yo). But it comes across entirely as an accident of apathetic design rather than something intentional—this is not, and I cannot stress this enough, [i]not[/i] a sublte game.

Note: also played on Sony Playstation 2 and Sony Playstation 4.

Updated Review:
Put 100_ hours into this to get full achievements, and I'll bullet point the most important parts.

Play this if
- You like the .hack universe and want to experience another aspect of it.
- You played it when you were younger, and you want a nostalgia bomb.
- You want to go back to the mid 2000s because it really does feel like it.

Don't play this if
- You want a tight action RPG
- You hate anime RPGS
- You want to play a great successor to IMOQ - because unfortunately I still believe the previous 4 games are superior and would honestly have preferred a rerelease of that.
- You want a hard game, aside from 1 difficulty spike in game 3 - the combat is easy, elements don't matter, magic is useless, and you'll never use a healing spell.
- You hate grinds

General notes
- If you use a PS3/4/5 controller -  there are mods to put the correct buttons in game. Bandai namco does not give you the option natively even though these games were originally made with playstation buttons
- If you're playing this on Windows 10, and sound seems to work EXCEPT you don't hear voices during cutscenes. What you need to do is change your speaker setup to Stereo.

All in all, despite my many complaints -  I don't regret playing it and recommend it with caveats.

Real time reactions with trapped chests (that's all so far, someone warned me they would be in the game, but that's all i see)

3 Notes for the Remaster:
-Remaster is mostly hd retextures without touching the core models and the combat system is identical to what it was in the 2002 release, from what I can remember, which means combat feels a bit dated and slow at times.
-Cutscenes got massive overhauls and redraws, pretty much updated to match modern graphics.
-English voice-acting wasn't changed is on-par with similar games from early-2000's released in North America, main character comes across very edge-lordy at times. Voices can be a bit cringy, but nothing worse than the average voice-acting for english dubs in anime, if you normally play JRPG's in english, this game won't be anything too diff or out of the ordinary from that.

For those that didn't play the original 2002-3 games:
-.Hack//G.U. is a game that you play as a top MMO player, the game includes both in-game MMO playtime as well as time where you log out and can access the MC's desktop, where there is a side TCG minigame based around the MMO's universe, an entire news app that updates to show in-world new broadcasts like youtube-videos, in-universe forums where you can download "fanart" (art that is part of the game shown as fanart), etc, to use as desktops or in-game avatars, icons, etc, and other unnecesarily detailed side aspects that you rarely are forced to interact with but exists on the side as added detail and lore
-The in-game MMO has a supposed 'random-gen' system where there is a couple of tilesets that you input generation seed's into to generate the area. There are 2-4ish tilesets per each game (Recode includes all 4 of the original games), so some ppl may find these tilesets get redudant or boring.
-There is several collection-type of side minigames and professions, including a guild shop you can have npc's sell items for you in and guild housing, ultimately meaning there is an almost disgusting amount of side content that you will be shown exists through the main story but never forced to play anything more than the surface of.
-The story itself was something that defined MMO's that break into reality and .hack was a universe that ultimately inspired later works like SAO with showing consequences of video games impacting reality, although .Hack//G.U. is a much different story from SAO. (And much older, not sure why I've seen anyone online say its a ripoff of SAO when SAO was published years after.)
-The game is long. As of writing this, I was casually playing and not focusing on completion, I was nearing the end of maybe 2/3 of the 1st game of 4, so itll probably be atleast 100 hrs for me to get through all of it.

I know the series since 2003. This is an excellent game, with an interesting story, beautiful landscapes and town hubs, enhanced by a stellar production team and incredible visual effects (for that time circa 2006) - - all of this, includes a dynamic and fast-paced combat system (one of the very best combat system I've seen up to now). However, it comes with some major flaws. 

1) The voice acting goes from ''well done'' to ''just ok'' - (not impressive), and most of the time quite annoying. You can feel that the voice actors really did their best to incarnate the characters. The producers really chose sharp and high-pitched annoying voices.

2) The cutscenes between chapters are very slow to get through. I skipped through the vast majority of them except for the Cinematograhic stuff. The cutscenes are 2X longer than necessary. You will see cutscenes at the main plaza, in the streets, at the Guild Hideout, when you interact with new characters and after bosses.

3) The dungeons get extremely repetitive ; there are only 5 distinguishable ''themed zones'' in the entire game. If I recall properly, in Volume 1, you have the Green Landscape / The Waterfall Caverns/ The Desert. Later on in Volume 2 and 3 you get access to the Desert zone and the Network zone. Yep - - that's it. Even .Hack/IMOQ had 8 zones all together.

4) Clearing the dungeons to 100% is an excruciating chore - - the distance between enemy groups is significant - in order to fully kill all the enemies in a dungeon (about 15 to 17 encounters, it will take you 45 mins to 1 hour, all depending on the circumstances and your strength level) - - And that's when you actually speed up your movement with spells and items.

Ugh, this game.  Let me list the cons on my playthrough first, because though I'm feeling particularly generous, this isn't a 'good' game by most metrics.

The bad:
To say the gameplay loop is repetitive would be the understatement of the century. 
The same 10 or so dungeon types are used without variation for your entire playthrough.
The story suffers from JRPG bloat on a massive scale. It's seriously the longest 91 hours I can remember playing. It just. Never. Ends.
The bosses are all relatively similar.
The anime melodrama is ridiculous, and Haseo is the definition of emo.
I only decided to play the (comparatively brief) 4th installment because I wanted my waifu of choice in a final cut scene, and whatever obscure thing I needed to do, I didn't, and I ended up engaged to the 'villain'. What the actual ****...
The combat...meh, nothing to write home about.
And the constant need to log in and log out to check email within the game was incredibly tedious and time-consuming.
Who the hell is this Tabby character that suddenly appears?
Oh and did I mention that for the first entire section our hero is a total jerk?

All of that said...
The good:
There's a nostalgic 2000's PS2 vibe here that's sort of undeniable.  I enjoyed the attempt to make this feel like an early MMO, along with fan art and old school forums.  The news and Online Jack anime segments helped to flesh out what was happening in the real world. And the characters despite the anime cliches are all basically winning (except for Haseo himself, but he improves over time), and the voice acting (on the Japanese side, I don't know about the English) is spot on. And its the rare game where I stuck with it to the end and maxed out my character, so that must say something.
The Sakubo character is actually pretty interesting from a psychological perspective (no spoilers).
The music goes pretty hard.
If you take a break, this game is good at hand-holding you back into the story.  I never felt lost.
Oh, and on the lowest difficulty, it wasn't too hard.

The verdict: 
This was a slog. There's no doubt about it. But in the end, I enjoyed finishing up my time in The World.  If you're going to give it a shot, play it a couple quests at a time and take breaks. Savor it. Because trying to binge this will probably wreck you...

When I first played .hack//G.U. back in the PS2 days, I was completely hooked. This was the fantasy for me—being inside a game world, messaging friends, getting emails, surfing a fake internet. It all felt like something out of science fiction at the time. I loved the characters, the world, the concept… everything.

I never got to finish the series back then. I made it through the second volume but couldn’t afford to rent the third, so I never saw how it ended. So when Last Recode came out, I jumped on it immediately.

Replaying it brought back so many memories. But I also couldn’t stop laughing a little—because the things I once thought were far-off dreams are now pretty normal. Minus physically jacking into a game, of course.

As for the gameplay? Yeah, it’s dated. Still fun, but easy to break. I found a way to level up fast early on, and after that, I was coasting through most of the game. The story still holds up, though. It’s engaging, emotional, and the characters are easy to connect with.

This remaster is definitely aimed more at fans of the original. If you grew up with it, it’s a nostalgia goldmine. But even if you didn’t, there’s still a good story here—just maybe wait for a sale.

Many aspects of this game have not aged really well. The gameplay is incredibly repetitive, the dungeon/field areas are very limited, side-quests are few and boring, the combat system is good, but subpar, and there's many mechanics that seem designed to waste your time (like not being able to just choose a city to log-in to, or login in to the game, see a cutscene, go back to desktop, to then log in again for another cutscene).

Vol. 4 is also a pretty good (if short, though I didn't mind it after around 70 hours on the other games) extra send-off to these characters and their stories, the new animated cutscenes are a blast and the whole soundtrack is still spectacular.

The combat is indeed nerfed and the entire experience feels too easy, but then again, with the whole grindy feel this pseudo-dungeon crawler RPG has, I actually didn't mind it much, because I would've quickly lost my patience otherwise (Forest of Pain tested my patience back then and I didn't complete it, only now being able to).

As for the port, it's a bit shoddy. It gets the job done, but you still need Special-K's mod to fix some stuff, and the draw distance is pretty pathetic. Not to mention I feel they could've polished a bit more, but it's no dealbreaker.

If you're an old fan, it's a chance to relive the games and a get a bit of an extra on the side. If you're new and like JRPGs, you're probably gonna enjoy it well enough too...just come in prepared to deal with a quite a bit of archaic design.

[b]Note:[/b] It is possible to like and enjoy the GU games as a standalone series; however, if you want to understand a lot of the references made throughout the games, it is recommended to have played the first game series and watched the .hack//roots anime. If you’re up to it, .hack//sign is also worth watching, as it’s the very first portion of the .hack// story. If you don’t have time for all that, reading a summary for each of them would still help. There’s also the Terminal Disc on the main menu, but not everything is unlocked right away; it has recap videos. 

[b][u]Very Important Suggestion[/u][/b] – If you’re able, use NVIDIA! You have to manually add the game to it and there’s even a lovely [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1505602960]guide[/url] with instructions on how to do that. IT MAKES THE GAME RUN [u]A LOT[/u] BETTER! Otherwise, it’s slow even on a decent PC. 

[u]Information[/u]
    • Haseo is also the main character of .hack//roots and this game series is directly related to what happens in that anime. 
    • As the series goes on, Haseo gets more party members and more weapons available to him. He only starts out with dual blades and zero party members.
    • Cheat Mode was added to the games for those who just want to enjoy the story. However, if you start a game on Cheat Mode, cleared data from a previous game cannot be transferred. This mostly means losing out on extras like BGMs and wallpapers. [i]You’ll also miss out on some achievements.[/i]
    • Dungeons are randomized (unless they’re story-related) and there are several different varieties of dungeons with unique scenery and enemies.
    • Enemies do not respawn. 
    • Equipment consists of weapons, armor, and accessories.
    • Leveling up is easy, because you can go to higher level dungeons as much as you want (within the server key words that Haseo knows). 
    • There are [strike]stando[/strike] Avatar battles, in which the Epitaph Users (Haseo and other special characters) can summon a [strike]persona[/strike] powerful entity unique to them. The key to winning those is watching for enemy patterns and knowing when to dash rather than attack.
    • The mini-game Crimson VS becomes available in Vol. 2. The key to winning matches is in the card line-up. Try to match characters that are related to each other to form a Delta Combo. The more you play, the better cards you’ll get. [i]There are a few achievements related to this mini-game.[/i] The cards feature characters and references from several parts of the .hack// story.
    • Vol. 4 is very short. It’s more like an add-on DLC story than an actual full game. 
    • There are “weddings” in which the characters’ player characters in The World can hold a superficial ceremony at a special location in the game. There are also platonic “Best Wishes” scenes if you’re not into romance. In the original, Haseo could only choose one, but in Last Recode, you’re given the option to see every single one (given that the character affections are high enough).

[u]Praises[/u]
    • Despite its short length, Vol. 4 was still enjoyable. I really liked the new weapon and skill moves. They’re seriously bada$$! I also liked seeing [spoiler]Ovan saved[/spoiler]. 
    • Excellent English voice acting. Practically the whole cast is full of some of my favorites. (Yeah, that’s right. I like English [i]dub[/i], mfs!)
    • Exquisite, beautiful music within the soundtrack. Probably one of my favorite video game soundtracks, ever.
    • In-game desktop has customization options for wallpaper and BGM. Each volume has a collection of wallpapers and BGMs that are mostly easy to obtain by accomplishing various things in the game. You can also re-watch cutscenes. 
    • Intricate (though a bit convoluted at times) storyline. It’s so enjoyable that even when you don’t understand something, you roll with it anyway. (Btw, it’s 99% Ovan’s fault for being cryptic and having crappy communication skills, if you don’t get something about the plot. ;) )
    • Could provoke thoughts and philosophies on artificial intelligence and even the future of video games.
    • Gameplay is very methodical, mostly because of the end-of-dungeon ranks you can get. It keeps track of how many enemies you defeated, how many items you got, how many chests opened, and so on. I find methodical gameplay enjoyable, so I thought I’d mention that for people who might feel the same way. It can be very addicting if you do!

[u]Complaints[/u]
    • Very slow, even on a decent PC. As mentioned before, use NVIDIA to correct this, if you’re able.
    • Scrambled controller button assignments. I use a PS4 controller. O = A. X = B. Triangle = X. Square = Y. Wat? Also, bumpers and triggers are reversed. Cannot be changed in game settings or Steam settings. The next time I play a game with Xbox 360 controller prompts, I’m going to have to unlearn what I had to memorize for this game. 
    • Cancel button randomly not working??? This only happened a few times, but it’s really weird. I’d be in a menu for items or whatever and suddenly the cancel button wouldn’t let me leave the menu. 
    • Inconvenient camera angles. Like facing away from the enemies a lot when entering battle. 
    • Pointless obstacles in dungeons, like spikes or swinging blades or lasers. They’re not fun or challenging. I just found them annoying because they slow you down, as though the length of the dungeon and the time it takes to defeat enemies isn’t enough.
    • Tedious collection campaigns. Like talking to all NPCs or meeting all lucky animals or saving Mecha Grunty so many times, etc.
    • The “highway master” campaign. UGH! I honestly thought I might not get 100% achievements because of those damn races. Terrible! Why would you put racing sh*t in a JRPG? 
    • Lack of racial diversity. Most main characters are pale and the few that aren’t are just tan. 
    • Uncriticized mild homophobia. While emailing Endrance, Haseo has options to be more homophobic, like saying, “Have you dated? A girl, I hope.” Then, if you choose to have a wedding scene with Endrance, other characters’ reactions are unsupportive. In the wedding CGs, Haseo looks uncomfortable with Endrance, but like, Haseo was the one who initiated the whole thing, so why would he look like that??? Point being, it turns gay characters into a joke. The devs had the opportunity to write a queer character in a good way, but didn’t take it. They could have had Endrance [i]not[/i] be unhealthily infatuated with Haseo, but instead gradually develop feelings for him for being supportive. But the devs had to be cliché and make it into a joke. Additionally, the character Hiiragi is repeatedly berated by other characters for being male in reality, but using a female player character in The World. 

Despite its flaws, I really enjoyed playing this series! It’s a super fun, addictive JRPG that I didn’t get to play on the PS2 back in the day, but always wanted to. I was really happy to see Last Recode when it came out; I didn’t even know they were working on that. 
I recommend it to anyone who likes lengthy – especially lengthy, in this case – JRPGs with light dungeon crawler aspects.

Review:
.hack//G.U. Last Recode is a collection of 3 substantial action-JRPGs all part of one contiguous storyline. The gameplay is reasonably deep; unfortunately, the game rarely provides enough challenge to players to force them to dig into the mechanics, even on hard difficulty. The story may not feel so unique and original in the age of Sword Art Online and its imitators, but it was pretty unusual at the time these games were first released, and the story is reasonably entertaining if you can ignore (or appreciate) some of the more cliched anime tropes. While nothing impressive for a modern game, the graphics are still decent and a significant improvement over the originals, and the game has an interesting aesthetic. In particular, some of the character designs are nice, although the models of some NPCs are reused excessively. The music ranges from decent to gorgeous, although a few pieces (such as the battle theme) recur so often that they can become a bit grating. And the dub for this game is mostly consistently good - enough so that it is probably worth playing with the dub for most people. Probably the weakest aspect of the games is the gameplay - while the games have decently robust gameplay mechanics for action-JRPGs, the games's relative ease means that there is little need to actually delve into those mechanics. For example, you character can learn many of the spells available to other classes, yet I only ever cast spells a handful of times during my playthrough and never encountered a situation were spells ever felt necessary. I must admit, this is a pretty difficult review to write. The game comes as close to "mixed" as I can get it, but it does end up on the positive side. So, without further ado, the details. 

The story is really innovative and interesting. The whole idea of "game within a game" hasn't really been exploited that much and the various twists are quite interesting and keep you immersed until the very end. I'd say the story, and especially the setting, is the strongest point of the game. 

The characters are a mixed bag. Some of them are very roughly drawn anime cliches, while others are actually memorable and non-trivial. The fact that you never learn the true faces and identities of the characters and only know their avatars only adds to the depth. 

The gameplay... at the start, I really enjoyed the combat system. It has the proper mix of engaging timings and fun abilities to make it interesting. However, the longer you play, the less enjoyable it gets. A lot of the later enemies are just reskins, and you basically only have a couple of basic enemy types. At some point, the game also becomes too grindy and too easy - I guess that on higher difficulties it would be more demanding, but then again I cannot imagine myself grinding so many battles on hard difficulty.

The grind. Oh my, the grind. The game's setting is a virtual MMORPG environment and I at some point I got the feel that it was really realistic and that I was grinding yet another of my WoW characters to level 120. And that is not a compliment. At least in WoW, the different areas have variety. Here, especially if you play all the parts in succession, it simply becomes tedious and repetitive. Why the authors decided that virtually all of the story dungeons have to take part in the same, "go through three levels" cave is beyond me. There is no autocombat feature like in Tales games, no autokill feature like in Persona, you just have to grind the battles. With the same reskinned enemies. With the same enemies on the entire level - sometimes there's nothing else than packs of the exact enemy in groups of 3, copied and pasted all across the level. 

Also, nothing ever happens in the levels. Nothing. No fun and enjoyable encounters, no extra sidequests, most of the storyline quests are "do the same tedious dungeon to the end of its 3-level glory and then watch a cutscene". The levels that are actually a bit different are also annoyingly spoiled - why would anyone think that figuring out a teleporter spiral is too hard for an average JRPG player and you have to drop obvious spoilers on their head?

The amount of copy-paste happening between the three episodes is sickening. How much can you play the [spoiler]basic story hook - go through the Arena championship - do random quests and dungeons with friends for character development - fight the supernatural foe[/spoiler] routine? You guessed it - three times. The exact same routine. Even the "quests" deal with exactly the same NPCs and open you up to exactly the same tedious grindy gathering routines.

Chim-chims - these deserve a separate point. Who in the world would thought that it would be fun to include an almost completely non-interactive, completely devoid of any skill factor resource system in the game that amounts basically just to going to clicky spots and clicking to get resources? At least add a minigame for it (no, chasing chim-chims or even running from the assassins does not count).

And finally, Episode 4. A giant troll. Basically a shortened, feature-reduced linear epilogue that toys with you by giving you some of the most fun combat mechanics (the final rank job extension) and then literally giving you one dungeon to run them in. It really seems like some of the feature distribution was completely wasted. Also, the [spoiler]Lost Weapons[/spoiler]. When you get them in [spoiler]Part 3 from the start, they are already upgraded to Level 3 - you get introduced to a new option to upgrade them only to learn that the upgrade requires fighting a... level 135 monster. Great. You'll get there after you beat the final boss. Then in Episode 4 they're upgraded to max again.[/spoiler]

In other words - this game has some really nice features. The "Crimson VS" minigame is actually quite enjoyable. However, it also has an absurd amount of tedious grind and an absurd lack of meaningful story content besides the main story. If you play it, I recommend treating it as 3 separate games. Don't do it like me and try to play it in one run - you'll probably get increasingly frustrated like I did. Otherwise, I'd say go for it (but I'd still check out some other titles first).

A PS 2 game which stood the test of time. Seriously, it handles far better than Alicization Lycoris -- with far more interesting cutscenes and character development.
-----
Combat is simple, spam normal attack button to chain long enough combo, trigger a "Rengeki" with a skill to increase your "Awakening Bar" which you can use to deal massive damage to enemies or increase your attack speed, then obliterate your foes.
...But, that's it, really. There's also a motorbike mini-game which feels abysmal in my opinion. 3D bullet-hell style game with obvious and repetitive bullet patterns. Which are repeated time and time again, making the game feels tedious, if not boring.
Oh, there's also an idle card mini-game, which is pretty fun.
-----
Supporting characters are also colorful and surprisingly lovable, with good character development. Atoli and Endrance are probably my favorites. Pi and Matsu are annoying. Silabus and Gaspard are just too precious. Yata just exists for expository dialogues. Zelkova is a deus ex machina. Kuhn and Antares act as mentors to the main character, Haseo. And a lot more characters with their own unique roles and identities further backed up with their own personal replies to your e-mail "greeting cards".
-----
World building is impressive, town is populated with... Uh, 10 NPCs or so with their own unique set of dialogues which develops as you progresses through the story, and their own unique inventory where you can trade your items with them. Giving the game an illusion of an MMO world. Outside the game, there's a news aggregator filled with eerily similar problems in our digital age (such as the digital divide, a notion to put microchips inside people, etc.) which was written in 2006, pretty impressive! 
There's also forums where people talk like people, trolling each other, supporting each other, sharing information for grinding areas/dungeons, etc. Seriously, I haven't seen any of this in other similar games -- even those published by Bandai Namco themselves.
-----
Graphics, ahh, good CC2 rendering. If they can just remake the whole game with CG-quality models, this probably would still hold up against modern games.
-----
And now, for the story. It's a typical anime story. The game assumes that you already watched the prequel anime, [i].hack//Roots[/i]. If not, then too bad, since you won't understand why Haseo have this questionable zeal towards Shino and Ovan. There's also a dude who e-mailed Haseo in the second volume, but Haseo seems to know that this dude already died sometime in the past -- even if this particular information has yet to be established in the game.
So if you want to understand the whole story, you've got to do this:
1. Watch [i].hack//Roots[/i]
2. Play vol. 1 through vol. 3 
3. Watch [i].hack//Returner[/i]
4. Play vol. 4.
So, yeah, a pretty shitty way to tell an overly complicated story, typical anime storytelling. Continuity errors also exists in those differing media, so you probably have to loosen up a bit (especially the ending part of Vol. 3 [spoiler]is different than the ending in the .hack//G.U. Trilogy movie[/spoiler] -- wait, scratch that, [spoiler]the whole movie is different than the game trilogy,[/spoiler] which is really annoying.)
-----
Next, I want to talk about localization. This game's localization is phenomenal. I prefer the English dub far more than the Japanese dub. Subtle things like the way Haseo shouts "Rengeki" when triggering it is far more weighty in English than in Japanese.
The voice actors also carries the whole game. Liam O' Brien's performance as Endrance makes the character far more authentic than it should be when compared to the voice acting in the Japanese version, and that just sells it for me.
-----
All in all, .hack//G.U. Last Recode is an enjoyable ride, albeit built upon a brittle foundation of another story-telling media outside the game in order to convey a full story.

A game that simulates an environment of an MMORPG. There are classes, levels, quests, servers, forum, PvP, PvE, and all that, but you are stuck with only one class since you can only play the main character, though you still get the chance to feel like you're playing four different classes at the same time—[spoiler]Haseo's class is Adept Rogue, meaning he gets to add some property of three other classes into one, and he also gets a hacked 4th form at vol 3[/spoiler]. 

Combat is easy but not simple, repetitive almost, yet strangely addicting. You mash a single button to attack, occasionally you'll want to guard, but mostly you just revel in the power of your skills. Whenever you see that REN-GE-KI or HAN-GE-KI, that's an extra shot of dopamine into your system.

There are lots of companions you can add to your 3-man party (and by lots I meant like 20+ people). Fortunately, you don't have to grind for their levels too much as they seem to scale based on the highest level member in your friend list. You also don't need to look for them as they will come to you instead—[spoiler]except for a certain character like Tabby that you can get in the middle of doing Forest of Pain event at vol 3[/spoiler]—sparing you the paranoia of missing a potential strong husbando or waifu.

There a lot of things in the game while at the same time there are very few things that matter. Gearing up is not a must but helps a lot since you can pretty much mitigate damage to non-existent. Lots of custom effects you can embed into your gear but few that are worth using. Nice bike effects. Nice guild features. Ryu Book is a chore but you'll have to do it anyway either for the achievement or if you don't care about achievement, at least get it to rank 4 at minimum (you can only reach rank 4 starting from vol 2).

You get lots of sidequests that give permanent stats boosting items. Some of them also unlock side campaigns. Side campaigns give little to no value items, save for few exceptions. This is because, by the time you clear them, it's likely you already level far beyond the requirement for the item. This is true for all volumes, whether you grind levels early on or simply following the story unless you decide to take some time to dedicate to completing the sidequest before leveling up too much (which is a bit of a grind and honestly, kinda pointless unless you aim for achievement).

There's also a mini-game, a card game called Crimson VS accessible once you're in vol 2. You tinker with it a little bit, get the cards that will ensure you a steady win rate, and then just leave it there like it doesn't exist until you remember at the end of the game that you need them for achievement or to become the number one in everything. This is even more true at vol 3 where you can decimate everyone with a single deck once you figure out the NPCs deck pattern. I have less than 100 losses on vol 3.

More things to grind if you care enough for the other [spoiler]Epitaph Users[/spoiler] including [spoiler]Adler's Key at vol 2 and Virus Core at vol 3[/spoiler] which isn't mandatory but kinda nice to have since you don't have to think about upgrading them with new ones.

[h1]Story[/h1]
[b]8/10[/b]

Watching characters grow throughout the journey, like proud parents seeing their child from afar. You start from playing in the lens of an edgy teen thinking he's cool because he's in all black and uses all these grim reaper-esque weapons turning into a [spoiler]mature young man shouldering the hopes and lives of many[/spoiler].

Even putting Haseo, the main character, aside. Most characters that make it into the story (except for those nameless, faceless, voiceless, useless extras) have interesting backgrounds, motives, principles, and goals (well, I don't know what is [spoiler]Gabi[/spoiler] even doing in the story) which makes them feel real. This helps in making them more likable and relatable in some parts (in my case it was [spoiler]Yata and Taihaku[/spoiler]). Particularly I like the story and development of [spoiler]Atoli, Sakubo, Yata, Alkaid, Sirius, and Ovan[/spoiler] the most. It is a shame that there are a couple of characters not fully fleshed out and just kinda Fade-To-Black before they return already changed a bit.

The plot twist behind plot twists as the secret slowly unravels itself towards vol 3 is worth the wait. Although I don't think it's difficult to figure out the mastermind and the big bad wolf behind the series of incidents that lead towards the end of the game.[i]Or does it?[/i]

Yet the story is not without flaws. The writer's effort to picture the emergency the characters are facing that is affecting the [i]real-world[/i] didn't reach me at all, it felt forced, incredibly forced. It makes much more sense to imagine that they are all living in a digital universe facing this threat that's about to destroy their world. Even showing me news of IRL incidents does nothing. [i]The World[/i] felt more real than the so-called [i]real-world[/i] in the context of this game.

The lore put into this game is massive. You have an entire section freely accessible that details everything about the races in The World and even their history. If you're into the lore and world-building stuff, it's definitely worth reading. It isn't necessary to know anything about it to play the game—[spoiler]there's a job extension quest in vol 2 that requires you to pass through the game lore quiz but you can simply choose all answer and pay cheap, easy to farm chim spheres when you answer wrong[/spoiler].

[h1]Social[/h1]
[b]-/10[/b]

No multiplayer or co-op feature.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
[b]7/10[/b]

A mixed reaction towards the graphic here. The cutscenes are all so good but other than those, it's somewhat weird to see faces that looked as if paint was slapped on top of a blank surface. If you look closely, you'll even find rare NPCs with a head that looks like it has been squashed. Characters feel and look blocky sometimes, especially when the camera zooms in after every combat. Add the mega-paint face onto that and you get a hella creepy living doll.

Many of the sceneries, however, are beautiful and unique. The World definitely has its own unique elements that make it stand out compared to some other fantasy settings out there. The Lost Grounds and the cities are particularly nicer ones to visit. Dungeons and Fields while pre-generated with limited environment elements has its distinct touch from one type to another (temple, underground, day field, night field). As far as I can tell, there are almost no elements in the building of The World's environment that is a copy of standard generic fantasy.

[h1]Audio[/h1]
[b]9/10[/b]

The music is absolutely gorgeous. I think this game deserves more praise for its music, underrated. Be sure to visit every single one of the [b]Lost Grounds[/b] within the game and also unlock every single OST through Ryu Book (oops, grinding time). Every character's OST is just as awesome, heck, even the soundtrack when you won a battle in the arena is nice. When you hear the character OST playing when Haseo is in a pinch, you just kinda go "Yeah!  is here!" or you might also go "Ugh. Why is  here."

My personal favorite music pieces are [spoiler]Hulle Granz Cathedral OST, World of Sin Ran Hati OST, Wailing Capital Wald Uberlisterin OST, Shallow Dreaming, and Hope of Dawn[/spoiler]. Not exclusively to the Lost Grounds, most pieces embedded into the game are a solid 8 to 9. Even the ridiculous [spoiler]Piros the 3rd OST and Mecha Grunty OST[/spoiler] are fun to listen to.

This game is not without its flaws and will likely be love or hate for a lot of people.  

The overarching story concept is great, though the writing leaves a lot to be desired (and some of the voice acting is obnoxiously bad).  Combat mechanisms are unique and interesting.  There is a large cast of characters that can join you as party members, but there is really no compelling reason to party up with most of them.  

The biggest cons to this game are the repetitive level design and the fact that it is extremely easy to become overpowered if you veer away from advancing the story at all.  

I would still recommend the game, particularly if you're a long-time .hack fan as I am.  I'd only played volume 1 on PS2, so this collection was a great find for me.

The greatest thing about these games is the unique premise for sure. In a general sense, it's a study of human behaviour in a simulated environment, how video game immersion affects one's decision making process, how freedom and restrictions shape the users' attitude and opinions, and how the online and offline world interact with each other. 

The in-universe MMORPG 'The World' is this hybrid isekai setting that smashed the 4th wall with its chainsaw-scythe, acknowledging fantasy and reality in the same space, appreciating and criticising the idea of escapism.  

The multimedia aspect of these games are actually really fun to observe. The most interesting part of the worldbuilding happened outside of the MMORPG, seeing the offline world's technological progress through news outlets and public forums. It's a fun lively way to recreate the pre-social media internet culture we had back then.   

All of this is background to a classic hero's journey, the main character Haseo goes through the same old story but the contexts are rearranged. 
It's digital instead of magical, divine powers are cheating tools, evil is not just cruel it's viral. 
It's cyberpunk under the guise of fantasy. It's great.

'Meandering' is the keyword here.

[u] Vol. 4 [/u]

It's a victory lap, return to this decade old world and give it the happiest ending possible. This is like Dragon Quest 11 level of optimism. It's nice.

Short Review: Strong story and worldbuilding, but boring gameplay.

Long Review:
.hack//G.U. is the 2007 continuation of the .hack series, introducing a new successor setting: The World R:2. Despite being a direct sequel to prior works, it does not require prior knowledge to fully enjoy -- in fact, I had only seen some episodes of .hack//SIGN in the mid 2000s before watching this. It is the first major series focusing on MMORPGs blurring the line between real and virtual worlds, about a decade before SAO did it. So how does it hold up?

The story is overall good, but the worldbuilding is absolutely fantastic. Your main drive is to save your friend who fell into a coma after being PK'd, and it's overall a treat for fans of MMORPGs. The story often comes in large chunks, with little bits put in around the end of minor quests. Throughout, however, you can check news feeds, six different forums, your emails, and even videos from ambush journalist Salvador Aihara to get a broader picture of what's happening around Haseo and the others. There is an immense amount of optional story that, especially in the first game, dwarfs the main story. These sources make this compilation a treat for people who enjoy story rich RPGs.

As for how the story compares to SAO? Despite similar themes, it's apples to oranges: .hack is like Star Wars while SAO is like Star Trek, because the former are Science Fantasy while the latter are Science Fiction. .hack has no grounding in the real world when it comes to any strange phenomena, involves religious concepts like AI deities and cosmic self-balancing, and ignores a lot of basic common sense when it comes to computing and hacking. SAO can mostly be explained in a realistic, near future scientific context. If you are fine with the mixing of the mystical with science, then you'll enjoy .hack.

The gameplay, however, is the weak link. The game's balance is absolutely atrocious. Levels make such an absurd difference that a 10 level difference can make the difference between one-shotting a foe or being one-shot. Item levels are virtually pointless -- I beat the second game with a mid-first game weapon at +5. Permanent stat upgrades are so overpowered that a migrated Haseo took no damage from mobs his level by the third game. Underleveled characters are fodder, especially with PKers whose levels center around Haseo's. The roguelike dungeons are lacking in features. The combat is oversimple and repetitive -- not even close to evolved as another, similar Namco series of Action RPGs: Tales. At a certain point I decided to just grind on dungeons 7 levels above Haseo and then curbstomp the story content.

The sound is a bit weird. The soundtrack is strong, leaning a bit on mysterious choral music. The English voices are a bit of a mixed bag. Atoli's voice is by far the strangest -- it may have been pitch altered at times and often sounds unnatural. Sound quality with voices also varies, suggesting that they weren't all recorded in the same studio. This seems to be cleaned up in the fourth game, as the voices sound crisper and Atoli sounds much more normal. The cast noticeably aged in that 10 year span, though.

I don't care about graphics, but they look nice. Clearly upgraded from 2007 standards so yay. Also, no apparent bugs from the conversion to widescreen.

Overall, it's best enjoyed by fans of story rich RPGs. The gameplay is shallow, but if this doesn't bother you, you'll like it.

[b]Gameplay – 6/10[/b]
.hack//G.U. Last Recode is a compilation and remaster of the original three .hack//G.U. games that released on the PlayStation 2, including an additional Volume and some bonus content. As to be expected of an action RPG of the PlayStation era, the combat system hasn’t aged so well. Tweaks have been made in this remaster to improve the flow of combat, but it still feels dated. At it’s core, .hack//G.U. Last Recode is a dungeon crawler. Dungeons are generated by using a combination of keywords. Keywords can be obtained from other players or by clearing dungeons. Personally, I like dungeon crawlers; they are repetitive by nature, so this might not be appealing to everyone.

I really like the Alchemy and Customization systems in .hack//G.U. Last Recode. Alchemy involves fusing matching pieces of equipment together to create a more powerful version, this gives an additional sense of progression beyond just the party level.  Customization allows you to add various effects and stat boosts to your equipment, this allows you to cater your party to your specific play style.

Experience scaling has been altered in this remaster. This massively reduces the amount of grinding required. I reached the level cap in the first two games very easily. I didn’t do any additional dungeons beyond the story dungeons and the keyword combinations provided via Email or forums. Levelling up so quickly removes any challenge that was in the original games. Increasing the Experience scaling, thus reducing the number of dungeons required creates an unnatural post-game grind. I had to do a lot of post-game grinding for the Chaotic PK’s, Lucky Animals and Mecha Grunty quests. Fortunately, this issue isn’t as apparent in the third game.

I love the way that these games simulate the MMORPG experience. I found myself recognizing NPC’s as I encountered them in various locations throughout the games. Having access to a huge range of party members helps emphasize this even more.

As previously mentioned, .hack//G.U. Last Recode includes an additional Volume. Volume 4 is much shorter than the previous three, I completed it in around 3 hours.

[b]Story – 7/10[/b]
I enjoyed .hack//G.U. Last Recode’s story. The game takes place inside The World, a fictional MMORPG and follows the protagonist, Haseo as he unravels the mystery behind The World players falling into comas.

Each game has a very similar story structure. The overall delivery of the story suffers because of this. By the end of the second game, I found myself losing interest in the story. Fortunately, the story really picks up in the third game.

Volume 4 wraps up some plot points that were left unanswered in the original trilogy. It was nice to see the main cast again and find out a little more about their lives following the conclusion of Volume 3.

[b]Visuals – 7/10[/b]
.hack//G.U. Last Recode does a decent job of remastering the visuals. Models and textures have been improved. The game supports 4K resolution and 60fps frame rate. Full motion cutscenes have been upscaled.

[b]Overall – 7/10[/b]
I enjoyed .hack//G.U. Last Recode and hope that CyberConnect2/Bandai Namco will give the .hack//IMOQ games the same treatment in the future.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
This is probably the best way to play these games. They are a bit easy, but it's hard to beat the price for these titles, especially when on sale. If you like video games about a video game, and that isn't low quality isekai trash, This game collection is 100% worth it. I'd actually recommend the english dub, as Yuri Lowenthal actually does a really good job in this one.

[h1]----Summary[/h1]
.Hack//G.U. Last Recode (what a title), is a game about a video game. You play as the player of the MMORPG "The World". Tragedy befalls you and you try to pick up the pieces of your life, and others' lives affected by the tragedy online and off. A lot of this game involves "dated" game lingo and people caring a bit too much about dying in an online game before it really matters, but I think that adds to its charm. Unlike most isekai trash, the real world matters as much as the digital one, even though you never really get to interact with the real world directly.

I especially like that the setting is a "futuristic" 2017 where VR is the most popular way to get online. The VR goggles are in a 4:3 resolution and aren't even 1080p. Amazing.

There is an anime that gives some context to the events that happen in the 8 months between the prologue and the main game, but you don't need to watch it, and it actually contains spoilers for a few plot twists. I watched it a long time ago, and remembered enjoying it, but I think you are doing yourself a disservice if you watch it first like I did. It's up to you.

[h1]----Positives[/h1]
[h3]Fully Featured Port[/h3]
This is one of the best HD ports of a PS2 game in quite a while. The game is in wide screen, HD, 60fps, and the upscaled textures (mostly) look good. You get both English and Japanese voice options in the menu, and all of the grind and many annoyances have been removed.

Other than a relatively low draw distance with pop in, very little texture/shadow weirdness, and the original quality video files for some cutscenes, you really get the best of everything.

The port is great.

[h3]No Grinding Necessary[/h3]
This is a big one. On the original release, you would need to spend some time leveling up in between main story missions. You would also want to do this to get more money, because the PS2 originals were somewhat stingy with the amount you earned. I can say that you [b]NEVER[/b] need to grind for anything unless you want to.

I would actually recommend against grinding unless you are trying to get to max level for the current game you are in, or going for end game content, as you can always continue the story when it becomes available.

[h3]Fun Action RPG Battle System[/h3]
If you've played the prequels, you will find that this game is more action focused. You lose some things, but overall I think I like the system better. There is something really satisfying about sending a monster flying into a wall, having it bounce off, and then doing another combo while juggling the monster in the air. It's not super deep, but it's more involved than selecting an action from a menu, though you can do that if you really want.

[h3]Interesting Lore and Setting[/h3]
Just like the previous games, there is a lot of supplemental lore involving the real world, and how technologically advanced things are. There is at least an hour's worth of lore before you even start playing the first game for real, if you want. From forum posts, to news articles, and even videos, you get a really good feel for the actual world the MMO takes place in. It helps the characters feel real when you see them offline because they have school or work or something, or when they comment on real world events like a new hypersonic train, or a plane crash due to network trouble.

I should stress you don't have to indulge in the lore, but it is "interesting".

[h1]----Negatives[/h1]
[h3]Grinding Even A Little Destroys The Difficulty[/h3]
There are a host of changes made to Last Recode which effect game balance compared to the PS2 games. You can look them up, but they contain spoilers, so be careful.

The game is kinda easy from a gameplay perspective, which is fine I guess. This game is definitely not Devil May Cry. What's not fine is that if you grind or do side content even a little, you will forever be over-leveled for the rest of the game. 

This is because they buffed the EXP gained from battles significantly. I played the "infection series" prequels on PS2 before I played G.U. and while I appreciate never having to grind for virus cores or levels like I did in that series, the fact that I basically can't do side content without ruining the rest of the game is a pretty big downside. I ruined the last 4th of the second game because I decided to do some side content. What I find particularly insulting is that there is a "cheat mode" built into the game that you can select when you start any of the games. It literally puts all your stats to 9999 making it impossible to lose. You don't even need it as even at the correct level, lots of monsters started hitting me for 0 in the middle of each game, because of the armor setup I chose. For some this may be a plus, but I don't really think it is.

The most fun I had in this game was taking on a zone 7-10 levels ahead of mine because I actually had the chance of dying. A hard mode where enemies have the same health, but do much more damage would be appreciated.

[h3]Dialog Pausing[/h3]
This is a relic from the PS2 era, when the PS2 had to read the audio off the disk. For much of the game, there are so...

many pauses between each line delivery. So sentences that should be...

one thought sometimes have awkward pauses, or reactions to something crazy...

will sometimes have an awkward delay ruining the scene. 

This doesn't happen too often, but you will need to get used to it. Anytime people aren't talking in a pre-rendered cutscene, you will notice. Weirdly, voiced dialog you advance yourself with a button loads fine.

[h1]----Conclusion[/h1]
If nothing else, I'm extremely happy this game doesn't over glorify escapism, video games, or embellish the player with isekai wish-fulfillment garbage.
