This JRPG 4-pack is an incredible journey; very few games can take this many hours of my life without garnering a sense of resentment, but this was special.  I can't say that I was left wanting more, but it didn't wear out its welcome, either.  Keep in mind that as big a fan of the genre as I was back in the Fourth and Fifth Generation (I didn't play much else back then), I've really fallen out of love with the genre, so there may very well be better ones out there that I just never picked up.  I also probably didn't play this the way that I was supposed to, so keep that in mind, but that also means that I had the freedom to even do that in the first place.  With most of my biases out of the way, let's get started.

The gameplay was pretty refreshing, and I don't know why more games of the era aren't like this.  Devil May Cry came around and revolutionized 3D Action, but it took other genres a while to try their hand at this type of combat system.  Like my beloved Rogue Galaxy, these games have a similar, but watered-down type of combat; you run around and slash at things in real-time, and the mechanics, while not all that deep, are pretty solid.  You've got your standard combo, your charge attack, and your over-the-top specials, and while that's mostly it, you can get enemies into a special state where your special moves do more damage and give everyone a bonus in experience.  Doing all that, you also fill a bar that lets you go into berserker mode.  There are tons of options, and your main character's warrior class is a jack of all trades, so you'll have access to several different weapon types over the course of the 4 games.  Your companions are controlled by AI, and you have a few basic guidelines to give them, which isn't a whole lot of control, but they mostly act intelligently.

The basic structure of the game allows you to dial in an address out of hundreds or thousands of possible combinations; dial it in to a level appropriate to your party, and go on an adventure!  There isn't a lot of variety - most of the areas are pretty cookie cutter - but all of the outside areas have different times of day, and what's there is designed beautifully.  Even though a lot of the areas look the same, I found myself getting really absorbed into the scenery, though mostly outside; the dungeons are neat, but not as pretty, and they're a lot longer.  Each area gives you a rank once you finish, but thankfully, how quickly you cleared it is not a factor; you can just take your time and do a good job.  Most equipment can be customized with extra goodies that give you benefits such as status ailments, elemental damage, and HP drain.  You don't really have to worry about grinding, either, because your levels skyrocket with little provocation; if you're looking for a challenge, keep on walking.  That said, there is so much to do: the game keeps track of which items you've possessed, which monsters you've battled, etc., and the more you do, the more your guild grows, which gives you extra benefits.  With that and all of the different quests available, there's plenty to do, and honestly, I found it fun just going on adventures to random areas, maybe even more than the story missions.

The actual story... well, it grew on me.  At first, I hated all of the characters (except the one who established early on that she's just OVER IT), but by the end of the third game, I found myself even getting attached to random NPCs that wandered around town.  I became genuinely happy for my extremely stereotypical shounen protagonist when people showed a genuine interest in his wellbeing.  Even some of the more annoying characters grew on me by the end, and with a cast this big, and an attitude as cynical as mine, that's no small task.  The actual plot has a lot of weird things happening, and not having played the other games or watched any of the anime, I was pretty lost at times, but almost everything comes together in the end.  If nothing else, it's a thematic departure from the usual settings of a game like this.

The environments, as I've said are beautiful, and the more unique elements of the game generally look pretty cool.  Most characters have some form of tribal tattoo on them, and they all look pretty neat.  In typical anime fashion, the main character's outfits get progressively more ridiculous, as do the weapons, but once I started to lean into that, I began to enjoy myself.  The monsters look very unique, especially the avatars, and even though some of them are a bit outlandish, they are very creatively designed.  Special attacks, spells, etc. are all appropriately flashy, and usually not too hilariously over-the-top.

The audio is pretty good; nothing really blew me away, but there's a lot to like here.  I didn't notice too much of the music, but the fields have appropriately serene music by day, and somewhat unsettling music at sunset.  A really nice touch is that at night or in the rain, there is no music, and you can just enjoy the atmosphere.  Most of the voice acting is good and not only fits the characters, but also frames them in a way that makes them work, not to mention that Liam O'Brien plays one of them, and that man is a national treasure.  You have a couple of duds now and again - one character sounds like a little girl making fun of how little boys talk [b]all the time[/b] - but they aren't too common.

If you're looking for something that's going to let you just pick up and go on an adventure at a whim, this might be up your alley.  I'm not a big anime fan, and despite that, I found myself really getting really into it.  I can't recommend it just for the extra fourth game that's never been released before; it introduces a few cool new things, but it's shorter than 5 hours, and in terms of plot, it doesn't add much.  That said, if you're looking to play these again, or are a newcomer (like I was), it's a pretty good value, and is pretty fun once you finally get into it.  See you in The World.

I recommend playing through it at least once if you're interested in a 2006 highly immersive game with iffy systems and don't mind some ps2 jank and barebones.

As for what content I completed. I did all the major quests including each volume hidden quest. Meaning I was able to do the Forest of Pain hidden quest (which gives you an extra ending on Vol 3, as well as connecting to the anime.). I also did the Crimson VS idle cardgame to be number 1 and beat the champion. Overall it was worth it, picking my favorite characters to beat the extra boss on each game was pretty fun.

EDIT: I've seen the anime and the RETURNER OVA. Was pretty good despite feeling a bit strange at times, specially seeing Haseo go back to his edgy self. I can see how it connects to the game as it ends exactly when we start Haseo's adventures. It also made me understand Tabby a bit more as the poor girl doesn't get any screen time here except for the game's extra quest and 100-floor dungeon, the Forest of Pain. Which was quite interesting as Haseo got his original powers from it as its hinted at multiple times. But this time... he reached different answers. As well as including some VERY plot relevant characters that are suddenly introduced in the game as if you knew them.

I'll speak about each volume one by one. There will be no story spoilers at all, so if you came looking for a good story I think its pretty great at that. At the bottom I'll write about the characters... and how I felt like they could've done more.

Volume 1: The first one. With our edgy protagonist Haseo. First I'll start with the negatives, since they may make you run away instantly. Gameplay is... simple and barebones, the combat is half-baked and the only depth it has is using the skills when the enemy glows purple or green in the pvp arena. You can block too to avoid getting knocked back. You get a two handed chainsaw sword later, but it sucks, then you get a proper greatsword, that also sucks because its slow, clunky and only has a combo of 2 attacks the second one charged, but the weapon deals so much damage and can hit downed enemies. As you may guess, I never switched back despite the twin blades being more nimble. You can't play as any of the other characters and you also can't decide what weapons to learn despite your class being able to do so. You take the role of Haseo. You are stuck with what he picks. That means as in the intro: Twin Daggers, Greatsword, Scythe. I was really, really disappointed when I learned that I can't play as other characters for variety, I can't even choose the weapons that the game obviously has. I love punching enemies when the game gives me the choice, sadly this one doesnt. Ooof. Sorry but it had to be said. It also has some really annoying and badly thought out filler quests, such as giving a flier to all 135 players in the game, kicking 50 lucky animals, rescuing Mecha Grundy like 150 times and so. And finally, I felt like they could've at least given the characters some mouth flaps and blinks on their textures when talking in cutscenes, many times they just stare at eachother with no emotion despite the VA doing a great job. 

Now enough of the bad. You may have thought that I dislike the game, that couldn't be further from the truth. If there is one thing this game excels at is at being immersive. One of the most immersive ones you can have. So after you play the intro you will end up in the Menu of your VR goggles. There you can browse the News and watch some videos such as Salvador Aihara, some world news, things that happened in the past and upcoming things (which for a game in 2006, they got a lot of things right as to what we have nowdays in 2024). You can also browse 6 different forums and even answer at some of the posts! These are very fun as you can see these players in-game, and seeing them speak about other stuff, the world, tips, area words etc is really cool! The ambience of the game is also quite well done and the OST is really fitting. I love Piros the 3rd theme. As well as the mysterious choir over at the Cathedral and so.

The story overall was a mixed bag for this one. I wasn't really enthralled by it, it was interesting enough for me to want to continue pursuing it as well as finding out about Haseo's past, as the game takes a timeskip early on. I'm not going to talk more about it as I personally think going in blind is the best way to experience it.

Volume 2: The gameplay is improved, making the Twin Blades and the Broadsword feel way better, the Twin Blades got their combo extended and the Broadsword got new charge levels for the neutral charge. This is how Vol 1 should've played.

Title: “.hack//G.U. Last Recode: Sword Art Online’s Cousin That Actually Makes Sense”


---

Hook:
“I came for a nostalgic anime MMORPG experience, stayed because I couldn’t stop yelling ‘WHY IS EVERYONE SO DRAMATIC?!’”


---

Key Features:

1. Story:
An immersive plot where everyone acts like losing in a video game is a world-ending tragedy.
“I’m trapped in a coma because of a game!” Sir, just unplug your router.


2. Combat:
Button-mashing brilliance that makes you feel like a god... until you realize you forgot to block.
Pro tip: Spam skills. Strategy is for losers.


3. Graphics:
They upgraded the visuals, but I’m still haunted by PS2-era cutscene stares.
Faces may look better, but the angst is still pixel-perfect.




---

Personal Experience:
“I spent an hour customizing my character only to remember... you’re stuck with edgy emo-kid Haseo for the entire game. On the bright side, his fashion screams ‘Hot Topic employee of the month.’”


---

Relatable Humor:

“The party AI: brilliant when healing others, but absolutely useless when healing me.”

“When I finally found that one rare item... only to discover it’s worse than the starter gear.”

“The email system in the game is so realistic that I started avoiding them in real life too.”



---

Pro-Con List:
Pros:

Deep story with twists and turns that make Game of Thrones look tame.

Nostalgia overload for anyone who remembers blowing into PS2 memory cards.

You can date your party members, because nothing says ‘romance’ like dungeons and trauma bonding.


Cons:

Haseo’s voice acting is 90% screaming.

Repetitive grinding. The enemies are sick of me farming them, and honestly, so am I.

Too much menu navigation. It’s like playing a PowerPoint presentation, but with swords.



---

Verdict:
“If you’ve ever wanted to experience an anime MMORPG without the actual crippling despair of losing to PvP players, this is for you. Just be ready to emotionally commit to shouting, ‘HASEO, NO!’ at least 20 times.”

This is overall a recommend based on about 90 hours of gameplay combined between a Windows MiniPC (AMD Ryzen 7 5875U, 32GB RAM) and a SteamDeck OLED 1TB. For background, I only watched the .hack/sign anime series and played the first game in the PS2 series when I was a kid. I am doing this rating after completing all 4 games. 

Overall, I give this a RECOMMEND but barely. I’d overall say 7/10. 

THE GOOD:
- Nostalgia: I do appreciate some of the connections to my childhood (Mac Anu, Hidden Forbidden Holy Ground, layout features, etc.). 
- Leveling system: I personally think they do a good job of trying to find different types of maps as you level up and go from game to game, so it feels like the dungeons are different but the overall concept/mechanics are similar. 
- Story; Story is okay, though I think they could have put more into the last game. 
- Memoir system: You can never really not know what’s next between the map and memoir, though this further encourages mashing skip through the crazy number of cutscenes. 

THE MEH:
- Amount/Balance of Cutscenes: Way too much and what’s the point because you can skip through almost all of them very quickly. It almost became an instinct by the time I had played it for maybe 10-20 hours.
- Gift System; The stupidest way to equip your party members. Why??
- Party System: It doesn’t really give you much reason to consistently use all of the characters. Some come and go but there are a couple early on that can carry you through Game 4. 

THE BAD:
- No cloud saves: This alone is a big hit. I have yet to own another game that doesn’t have cloud saves. Just not forgivable and also keep in mind if you uninstall and haven’t backed up, your data is gone. 
- Optimization is terrible; The lag on my PC is the absolutely stupidest thing ever. Lumina Cloth was laggy as hell (and you spend a long time there, fun). All of the Skeith fights, including the final one, and many bosses were stupidly laggy. Imagine playing through 3/4 games on a laggy as hell PC only to  find out that the SteamDeck runs the game flawlessly, but have to cope and play the last game BECAUSE THERE ARE NO GD CLOUD SAVES!!!

So overall I think the game has a cool story (if you don’t fall into the temptation to skip the cutscenes). I would BUY IF ON SALE but NO WAY JOSÉ AT $50 PAL.

590.7 hours. That’s how long I spent inside “The World.” I laughed, I cried, I screamed at corrupted save files, and somehow... I still want to dive back in.

This game is special. It’s not just nostalgia — it’s an [b]experience[/b]. The story pulls you in, the music hits deep, and even though the gameplay can feel repetitive, I never got tired of it. I got so far into the game — nearly to the last chapter — only for my file to get corrupted. Yep. 590 hours gone. Just like that. I stared at my screen in silence, questioning my entire existence.

But here’s the crazy part — I still want to start over. That’s how much I love this world. The story, the characters, and that emotional connection you build with Haseo and the crew make it totally worth it. The music alone deserves its own award — it’s atmospheric, emotional, and perfectly fits every scene.

The combat system isn’t the smoothest, but it gets the job done. I was way more into the story and the vibe anyway. The visuals are polished, the art is clean, and it’s wild how good everything still looks for a remaster of a PS2-era game.

If you love anime-inspired RPGs with deep storylines, memorable characters, and that nostalgic MMO vibe, this game will grab your heart and never let go. Just… back up your saves, please. Learn from my pain.

I have no child memories or nostalgia toward this game what so ever. Which is good because I'm here to try and convince those like me to give this game a chance. Also this is a long game series so my review is going to be pretty long as well. 

I do recommend this game, with some suggestions before you buy it though. First there is an anime call .hack//roots that serves as this game's starting point. and there is a anime called .hack//SIGN and 4 other .hack games. You don't need to watch the anime .hack//Sign or play the other 4 games to understand whats going on. The game comes with a mode that gives you a nice in game lore rundown so you can understand it if you want, but ultimately it will not keep you from enjoying the game only enhance an already good experience. Now .hack//roots however I do recommend watching since its about the main character and gets your more emotionally invested into the character. Who is designed to be a jerk for the first half of Vol. 1. You don't need to, but i still recommend if you have the time. Keep in mind the anime is more character and drama than action, while the game has a healthy balance.

Now that is out of the way lets talk about the game itself.
Game play is archaic by modern standards which will be hard for some who see more modern action RPG's as the standard. 
I still found it fun and its the least grindy JARPG I have ever played. And if you don't want grind and just want to see the story the game comes with a cheat mode that there for you to complete it as fast as possible. 
Graphics are what you expect from a early 2010's game. The don't become noticeably better till vol. 3, probably because Pie took most of the budget for a couple of scenes ; ) .
They captured the feel of playing a MMO as close as they could without it being an actual MMO. All the extra content you can look into when you log out in game is honestly amazing. The amount of extra work to get 2d animations for news and other events. Forums of people chatting and characters behaving like what you expect some people would on the internet. And some real surreal stuff in the in game news showing a pretty damn accurate prediction of our modern society.

The writing is really good, but its not perfect, seldom any game is. If I were to give it a grade it would be a solid B. 
    Reason 1: A lot of interesting side character knowledge, not development, but specifically things like a characters like and dislike and even backstory can only be learned through a greeting card system. Which you are given a limited supply of. Its a real shame you can't talk to the characters normally or have more cards to learn these facts about them.
    Reason 2: OVAN, OVAN, OOOOVAAAAAAAAN. I literally have no idea after playing the game to 100% why Haseo, as my friend describes it, rides Ovan's d*** so much. You who are new to this series will also be perplexed as to why as well, for even the veterans can not bring a satisfying reason, other than I never had a decent father figure so I settled. Haseo is not the only one who has this problem, but lets move one.
    Reason 3: Vol.4 was added years later to celebrate the franchises anniversary and to give the OG fans something as well. The reason it hurt is story is because of Ovan. you will understand when you get there.
    Reason 4: Ovan. The best way to describe Ovan to some of you is imagine if you combine Sasuke and Itachi from Naruto and create someone with half the cool and motives of Itachi and half the b*** and motives of Sasuke. And Haseo is Ovan's Naruto. With all the fan fiction that fallows such a comparison to prove it.

Now lets go over the positives briefly so as to not spoil anything, so I don't ruin any surprises or leave the wrong imprison.
The overwhelming amount of characters in the game are all likable in their own way and some go through a lot of character development. Haseo the main character going through the most and its very satisfying. One character you will hate more than anything and its perfect because that is the purpose of the character. There is plenty of heart warming and hilarious moments in game.

Lastly the game comes with a parody mode which is an abridge of certain scenes voiced by the characters voice actors. A nice hilarious reward for finishing each volume.

Is this game worth 50$? Yes, it has more worked put into it than most AAA RPG games that come out today. But if you can wait or need to save money, then no harm waiting for a sale.

.hack//G.U. Last Recode consists of the three PS2 .hack games in one collection plus an additional and final 4th episode.  This is a unique JRPG.  Without spoiling game structure, you boot up the game but you're not in the game.  There are various supporting interfaces to add realism.  The games show their graphical roots with low poly character models, however the games look good in high definition when played on modern hardware.  

Not to look a gift horse in the mouth, at least the characters are voiced however the their mouths don't move except in a few scenes developed for the PC release.  The option is there for Japanese voices which add an air of authenticity however using English voices the game still forces English sub-titles.

The leveling in this series is completely defective if not mutilated for the PC release.  The story missions don't scale to the protagonist's level.  This wouldn't be the first JRPG with these issues.  Since this is a repackaged release, perhaps something could have been done to fix the story missions to make them on par with the players level.  I've found the sweet spot in ad hoc battles to exceed the protagonist's by about seven levels.  For much of the game you are and in many cases severely over leveled.

The level disparity ruins many mechanics of the game.  Items, buffs, potions will sit in your inventory while you yawn through battle after battle.  The only exception is the word based battle creation system used to create non-story battle arenas, however, with higher level battle arenas you find yourself in the same situation gaining levels at a massive rate which further exaggerates the leveling problem.

Another issue is the limited number of battle arenas.  Fields and dungeons where the battles take place all look alike and are only differentiated by layout.  Not helping is that the battle system is a one button press except for one special move indicated by a visual prompt and another initiated after generating enough morale for your battle party.

In sum, the story is very engaging and worth engaging with.  I'm near the end of the 2nd game and honestly need a break from the tedium.  YMMV!  Engage with these unique role playing games but take a significant break between each and you'll find your purchase worthwhile.

What can i say? 

It's not, that the game doesn't run properly...it mostly does. 
It's not, that it doesn't look good...it mostly does. 
It's not, that it doesn't feel well designed...oh, it somehow does. 


The game: 

First, i thought it was me only, but noticing others considering alike...it feels like the hours spent within the game, feel the equal of days on your mind. 

Softlocked conversation-options with tiring dialogues, which are badly timed (many - way too long - gaps in between the characters reacting towards other character's sentences, EVEN when they are interfering/interrupting them), causing you to log in, go there, do that, log out, check mail or forum, relog, etc., do some story-related quests, locked behind other story-related conversations...rinse and repeat. 

The characters are flat/hollow, the conversations are boring with some funny moments...i only played Part 1:Rebirth and "only" for about 8 hours, my char is - though grinding for XP - level 11, getting about 12XP among average monsters of story-related quests and 40XP per won match among arena-fights against level 13 oponents...and it "only" takes 1000XP to level up...do the maths. 

Maybe the average outcome might be higher in some random dungeons/"teleportation-bookmarks", but i'm not willing to shoulder the frustration of finding out, it won't be. 


The story: 

The whole thing itself is not bad...and - as it seems - it's based on an anime-series and THAT exactly is, how the script feels like. So i guess, it's a nice anime, but adapting this design resulted in an extremely struggling game. 

I just can't recommend anyone wasting away so much money (if you have to, get it on high discount or in a bundle), time and growing yourselves headache. 

The game feels empty and somehow - whenever i play it - i do as well. 
Though the plot is likable and quite "reknown" on similar products like "Sword Art Online" or . "Log Horizon"...you know...virtual world, real world, ingame character leveling and questing. 

I guess, you have to be very young and unaware of the downsides, to really enjoy the game, because you might consider "time" different, then you do as a mature teenager or adult. 



Conclusion: 

I once tried to play a game named "Grandia 2", i'd give this one the nickname "GRINDia" instead. 

"Final Fantasy" 7 to 9 feel way more enjoyable, just like other JRPGs like "Code Vein" (!beware! soulslike mechanisms) and "Scarlett Nexus" also did and leveling can be quite tricky there already. 


So the product itself is alright...nice visuals (referring to the age of the game), beautiful cinematics (as commonly used in good JRPGs), suitable voice-acting (English), seemingly solid coding (had no crashes, bugs or glitches), but some mechanisms, the storyline and the enforced conversations just slow and drag you down. 

So i might be tempted, to check out the anime, if i ever get my hands on it, but i hate, not being able, to appreciate the game alike. 


The "missing recommendation"/negative review mainly is, due to the extremely slow "progress" and the tiring conversations. 
I wouldn't wish my worst Nemesis to be forced, playing this game-series through completely...or would i!?  

If you don't bother these downsides, i hardly could find a reason, not to recommend it, with what i experienced. 

Most people though prefer hard grinds in different kinds of games and the focus of a JRPG more story-progress-friendly.

I loved the game when it was first released for the PS2, but sadly the repetitiveness of the combat/dungeons hasn't aged well at all. Those that have played it, even the most die hard fans, know what I'm talking about. For those that don't, there are a grand total of like 4 dungeon types, that all look the same but just have different layouts. The combat never strays from "smash this button repeatedly until a specific moment arises, then hit this different button". It wears out its welcome after the first 2-3 hours.

Also, I'm not sure whether the creature comforts of modern gaming are coming into play here, but having to leave "the game" each time I need to check email/forums/etc is so clunky and cumbersome. To make matters worse, they even add an artificial "loading" bar to every option in the "computer menu" just to make it even more of a hassle. To top it off, I even encountered a moment where I logged out to check all the above, then the moment I logged back in I got another email, which I then had to log back out to check. Oof. 

Then there's the issue of mouths not moving during in-game graphic "cut scenes" (except for the very, very rare super up close instances, which shows they could have if they wanted to). I realize it was this way in the PS2 release as well, but there were times I found myself wondering who was even talking until I got acquainted with all the voices. You don't want to add mouth movements because it would be too much work? Fine, but at least add the name of the person speaking next to their dialogue. 

Finally, the extra volume. It's... not very interesting, at all. Not to mention it's very short and just kinda seems tacked on for the sake of saying "here's something new". It truly adds very little, if anything to the overall story of the series, and feels more like a marketing tactic to sell units rather than anything of importance. 

In the end, honestly I only bought the game to show support in hopes they release a new .hack series in the future. The story isn't bad at all in the grand scheme of things, but the entire experience is marred by poor combat and clunky design. I recommend removing the rose tinted glasses, and only picking this one up on sale -- and only to support a possible future release.

Let's start with the good things. The atmosphere is amazing. It ACTUALLY feels like you're immersed in the world of The World (haha... sorry, i'll see myself out)

Somewhat of a middle ground are... The characters. DEAR LORD, how annoying almost everyone is, ESPECIALLY mc Haseo himself. I think it's the first time ever I've hated the protagonist so much. Fairly sure the writers had a competition of who's going to make the edgiest and asshole-est character possible, and I can say for sure they did deliver. I do know the full story of a game, I know all about his reasoning even though I never finished the trilogy, but even so controlling the most uninterested in video games angry online gamer ever felt like driving a car without brakes on a downhill road - the guy is so much of a jerk you can't relate to him even if you try.
Credit where credit's due: deuteragonists and other side characters you actually interact with fit all the tropes but still manage to feel like real people you would meet in an online game, each with their own personality, motivation and yadda-yadda... Buuuut even though they have some depth to them, it's still more like 2.5D with no real third dimension to them. For example, the twins are a good concept that was kinda poorly executed.

The worst part: gameplay. As I said in the beginning, every single scene is drawn out. Awkward pauses, repeated delivery of the same information, constant need to log out and log back in just because of some mail... Then there are the party members you don't actually need, relationship system (which, while well implemented outside of combat, still urges you to just hit those finishing strikes every single time just to max it out. like, come on, show me a single person who'll start loving me due to the fact i managed to pummel a virtual teapot), sidequests that require talking to every single character in the game (gotta be honest, i do that in JRPGs anyway, like talking to every single NPC i meet in Kiseki or Tales, but that's because they usually ARE interesting to talk to, not just "DID YOU KNOW THAT ENEMY CAN HAVE A WEAKNESS". damn, talking to people in FF is more interesting than those walking cardboard cutouts). 
The alchemy system is really not deep at all. The equipment all feels the same. The skills are... well, bland. Trading with other characters is great, but pretty much useless. Randomly generated dungeons are BOOOORING. Not like grindy boring, more like text-based games feel like they are filled with action next to those stupid corridors and square rooms populated with groups of three to five mobs.
How exactly do the players manage to play the game without gaining any levels at all? How does one walk around the world populated with enemies four levels above them and never get into a fight with any of them? What do they actually online if they don't participate in anything the game has to offer? G.U. doesn't appear to be written outside of the necessary world building and story canvas it needs to deliver the plot to the player.
It wasn't really a good RPG even for the time it was released. Damn, 2006 had Oblivion, Grandia, Suikoden, Kingdom Hearts 2, and so much more...

And yet even due to all the shortcomings, due to the fact the game feels outdated in 2017, it still is genuinely a good experience.
Buy it during the sales if you've never played it.
Buy it for full price if you played it some years ago and consider refreshing it in your mind.
Feel the nostalgy. Embrace The World.

Title: A Glitchy Grindfest That Deserves Better

Review:
.hack//G.U. Last Recode is four games bundled together—Rebirth, Reminisce, Redemption, and Reconnection. On paper, that makes the $50 price tag seem fair. But honestly, this remaster feels more like a relic that aged poorly than a celebration of the series.

First off, the technical issues are brutal:

No cloud saves (thanks, Bandai, for removing them for some ungodly reason).

Frequent crashes, often during scene transitions or critical story areas.

Huge risk of losing hours of progress, or even your entire save.

Buggy freezes that feel more like bad coding than the “rogue A.I.” storyline.

Gameplay-wise, it’s monotony wrapped in nostalgia. The combat is basically a stripped-down Tales system—okay at first, but quickly stale. Nearly everything funnels you into endless copy-paste dungeons. Need info? Dungeon. Want a boss fight? Dungeon. Trying to progress story dialogue? Yep, dungeon first. Grinding isn’t optional—it’s the backbone of the design.

Story & Characters:
The premise is cool—stopping player killers in an MMO-gone-wrong has superhero vibes. But the pacing kills it. Vol. 1 in particular drags with back-to-back tutorials and a tournament arc where every single match is robbed from you by cutscenes. Characters aren’t bad, but generic; they feel like archetypes you’ve seen in 5+ other JRPGs. The “coma from playing a game” storyline works if you squint and accept “because magic.” Otherwise, it’s pretty juvenile.

There are some good moments—the avatar fights are exciting, Atoli’s crush on Haseo has its cute beats, and the overarching narrative has potential. But the grind, pacing issues, and technical problems bury it.

Personal Take:
I stepped away multiple times out of sheer boredom—ended up playing 7 Days to Die, Pokémon ROM hacks, Hot Wheels & Lego rides with my kid, and Diablo IV with strangers instead. That says it all. As of 8/19/25, I officially retired this game and deleted it from my backlog.

Verdict:

As a movie? Solid 6/10—watch the cutscenes on YouTube or revisit the anime.

As a game? 4/10 at best. Tedious, buggy, and outdated.

If you want to experience .hack//G.U., you’re honestly better off emulating the original PS2 versions on PCSX2 than wasting time on this watered-down remaster. This deserves a true remake, not this lazy port.

Would I recommend it?
❌ No. Not even on sale. I wasted $20, don’t repeat my mistake.

I've always had a soft spot for the .hack series of anime, especially .hack//SIGN and .hack//Roots. While I don't consider either of them to be amazing, they are conceptually original and it's interesting how they were delivered to complement their video game counterparts. And in the case of .hack//G.U. Last Recode, .hack//Roots is the anime counterpart - I'll refer to them as GU and Roots from here onwards for brevity.

It's hard for me to decide whether to recommend this title or not given my slight bias towards the anime series. So instead, I've decided not to recommend based on the fact that this game hasn't aged well (at all). The graphics and 3D models look very dated; and the action combat is clunky and not very engaging. This doesn't mean it's a bad game, it's just not good by modern standards for a video game - but it's definitely more than just playable as long as you can tolerate the gameplay of older console games. 

You'll be playing as an unnamed main character who plays an MMO game, "The World", and whose in-game character name goes by "Haseo" - it's a "game-within-the-game" concept. You'll have access to in-game mail, forums, news site and the MMO, with which you'll often be switching to and fro as the story progresses - much like a simulation of real-world (but without multiple displays because you're gonna need to logout from the MMO just to read mails, etc!). When you logout of the MMO, you are presented with a desktop screen (a simulation of an operating system) which is used to access said features. The story revolves around mysterious incidents of players (of The World) falling into comatose (in the real life) which is somehow connected to the game.

Despite my not recommending it (I'm really on the fence here), I think there's something that can help you decide more easily. You will be thrown into time 8 months later shortly after you begin playing GU. The anime, Roots, is about what happens during this time gap (as a prologue) and you can watch it to see if you're invested in the storyline - youtube has some dubbed episodes (but might not be a complete collection). A word of caution, however, is that the anime is more philosophical than action-oriented. I've actually rewatched Roots just to recap the earlier story. While it's often said that .hack popularized the "Isekai" genre in animes, it isn't parallel/alternate worlds and is very similar to Sword Art Online but with a more extensive backstory (though I don't think either series had inspired each other).

If you liked the anime, I recommend getting the game for a continuation of the storyline as it is well-delivered in the game. The voice-acting (both Japanese and English dub) and pacing is pretty good although it can feel like a slow burn and text/cutscene heavy. The game consists of 4 volumes and is down to 90% discount when on sale. I should also mention that the game includes video summaries of the quadrilogy before GU (referred to as "IMOQ"), to provide some context relating to The World up to this point.

If what you care about in a JRPG is primarily story and immersion (i.e. everything else is secondary, or can be overlooked), I think GU is an above-the-average JRPG title. The story is good and still holds up well, with a balanced focus on both plot and characters. If you liked the type of stories in Persona series, I find the story in this game to be pretty similar. If you're acquainted with the .hack series, you'll also find characters in the game that connect back to earlier games/animes, which I found to be a nice touch. There's also humour every now and then which can be easily appreciated by any self-respecting weeb (disclaimer: I play on Japanese dub). The music is good too where immersion is concerned, though not at the level of its earlier anime counterparts, which without a doubt, had contributed greatly to the popularity of the series - like "Key of the Twilight" by Yuki Kajiura, or "Dwindled Bible" by ALI Project, as examples. My favorite song in GU is "Gentle Hands" and a couple of other BGMs that stood out to me are "Eternal City Mac Anu" and "Celestial City Dol Dona" which are played when in town. As a side note, if you found "Gentle Hands" pleasing to your ears, you should definitely also check out "You smiled kindly" and "Carl's theme" - I rotate between these 3 as BGMs played when in the desktop screen.

Now, if you didn't like the anime (or don't like anime at all), then I suggest skipping it because the main attraction here is the story and world-building, the rest are pretty mediocre. It's also filled with anime tropes which most people either love or hate.

Regardless, I am having fun with GU because I've watched the anime long time ago (and liked it) but have never played the game. But I feel that both GU and IMOQ deserves modern remakes; especially IMOQ, which I feel is far superior (story-wise) but is even clunkier in terms of the gameplay. So here's hoping that Bandai Namco would one day decide to remake the 2, so that I no longer need to hesitate about recommending them. Ironically, for a game that I didn't recommend due to its aged graphics and gameplay, it's a new entry in my favorites list.

P.S. There's something about Haseo that is neither explained in the game nor in the anime. However, he does have a relationship to past series (as with many characters you meet in the game) which I'll leave to you to find out on your own. ;)

[b]A review based on first 8 hours of the 1st game:[/b]

Q: [b]"Is it an RPG?"[/b]
A: Not really.

Q: "Did they expect VR goggles would feature "Standard 1280x1024 full-color* display" in 2017?"
A: Yup, they sure did. Gotta give them props for at least getting the full-color part right. I mean, I'm sure y'all remember what % of TV's in 2017 used to be black and white. (I am being sarcastic.)

*For those who don't understand what "full-color" means: Back in the olden days, there were monitors / TV's which didn't have proper colors. Some were black and white or had a very limited range of colors it could display.


Q: "But isn't this supposed to simulate an MMORPG?"
A: I dunno. I doubt the developer / designer had ever played an RPG game before.
The characters make awful decisions that never should happen in an MMO. 

1. You don't get to "roleplay", aka you have like no influence over your character. Your character says what they want except during minor email conversations where you get to choose if you wanna ask about Y thing or X.
2. There's no character building. You don't get to design your class. Leveling up doesn't let you alter anything about your character. (There's no perks, skill points, ability points, new abilities unlocked.) Leveling up is just a passive boost to stats like HP, SP and ATK.
3. There's only 3 item slots. (Ring, weapon and armor. No shields. No "X weapon in 1st hand, Y weapon in 2nd hand.)
4. Armor doesn't change your appearance. You won't be changing how you look. 
5. Within the first 8 hours you can expect to equip 1 new weapon and 1 new armor, neither of which change anything about the gameplay.
6. There's 1 slot within each equipment to add a thing to it. "+10% less phys dmg", "+50 SP", "Inflict Poison on Atk (sometimes)"
7. Poison is a 1 dmg tic, not a max hp %-based tic. So in later game you can deal like 10 dmg using poison every 10-20 hits or just hit them once for like 200 dmg. (A lot of equipment/items in the game are worthless and impractical.)


So basically:
1. It's not an RPG. (Either laziness from devs or incompetence.)
2. It has low player agency. (Can't influence how stuff goes.)
3. Also, you might find this game's writing some of the most cringy stuff ever.
4. Also, the combat doesn't feel particularly fun or great. Often you'll wanna avoid fights since it's not enjoyable. Though, you might go find over-leveled enemies now and then so you get better loot and more exp so you minimize the amount of time spent fighting in the game. 
5. Some of the optimization is absolutely horrible and will suck 100% of your GPU usage for no reason when you're just in a menu looking at some .pngs or .jpgs. Enjoy having your GPU turn it up to 80 C (176 F). If you're living somewhere warm, you might wanna play with a fire extinguisher near you.

It's a lazy, poorly designed unintentional comedy due to how awful the writing often is.

Q: "Why should I play it?"
A: You might wanna laugh at how stupid it is or how awkward stuff is.
I guess the hope of finally being able to Data Drain annoying NPC's (such as Atoli and some pig furry) is a compelling motivator to play it.
(Data Draining is like banishing people to the Shadow Realm or making them lose all their stuff in the MMO and be set back to level 1.)
Hoping the protagonist will finally snap and begin griefing others until they stop playing the game and leave you alone gives me hope.

This game is awful.  Absolutely awful.  Completely unbalanced, terrible characters, and .hack// seems to suffer the same problem as Aliens in that every single piece of media tells the same basic plot over and over and over and over.  The only redeeming factor this collection has is that it's at least the full game at one price instead of making you pay full price three times over to get a full game's worth of content (and, no, each individual piece is NOT a full game's worth).

To get into specifics, the game is completely unbalanced.  The amount of experience you get from enemies is mostly flat the entire game, only determined by your level, and the enemy's level.  Unfortunately this is ramped so high that you generally can level every 2-3 fights.  One dungeon can have a few dozen fights.  The maximum level is 50 per game (so 50, then 100, then 150).  I gained 8 levels in one dungeon run.  So you can massively, massively outpace the story without even trying, you can do it simply by doing the side quests.  On top of that, the damage you do has more to do with the level differences as well than your gear.  This is supposed to make it harder to go to a dungeon that's too high for you, as you'll do minimal damage, but ultimately you really can keep enemies locked long enough to kill them anyway even with a sizable difference.  Not that you need to go after high end enemies.

Gear drops don't match the level of the dungeon either, despite what the game tells you.  Your NPC party members can gain quite a bit of levels as well, to 'catch up' while you're not using them.  However, they won't do anything about gear.  You can have someone join your party in the 30's still wearing level 1 gear because you and you alone determine what they use.  In most RPGs this wouldn't be such an issue, but this game is pretending to be an MMO.  But the other characters are dumber here than in most other RPGs anyway.

The story is laughably bad, the same rehashed plot line of "there's a glitch/not-glitch in The World that gives some users super powers and puts other users in comas" and you're the CHOSEN ONE who also has the power so you can counter it.  But the characters in this are absolutely insufferable.  Their personalities are extremely poorly written to the point of parody of religious zealots, pacifists, psychopaths, and the like.

The game is a train wreck on every level.  The original PS2 RPGs (not the G.U. but the set before it) were not masterpieces but they were significantly better than this.  Even the concept of the three keywords just doesn't work well in this, the dungeons it creates are even more lackluster than the original set's.  There's no real incentive to play them either since you'll just end up so far ahead of the plot that nothing matters, you may as well be using the game's built in cheat mode.  For the record, no, I am not using that.  I wanted to actually play the game.  But there's no game here to play.

This game belongs on "worst of" lists.  Just avoid it.

I used to love PS2's ./hack//G.U. series and had high hopes for this remastered version.
However, it was a complete let down.

Some old flaws are still there, such as every time you go to a city a handfew of NPCs are assigned to be around you and even if you teleport to another part of the city, you'll see those same NPCs.
But new flaws have also been introduced, such as the "boring mode": forget about feeling like you are in a MMORPG, just insta-kill every monster. And no, I'm not talking about the "cheat mode", whatever that is. I chose to start a "normal game" and Haseo is so OP, battles are a complete waste of time.

I stopped playing as it became a graphic novel with lots of overhead.
There were no improvements other than some slightly better textures.

If you're an enormous fan of .hack, have a huge amount of nostalgia for the series, or want to play the 4th part, go ahead and buy this.  They did an excellent job porting the games to PC and I encountered no issues whatsoever during my time with .hack (hunt around for the v-sync option if you get screen tearing).

The reason this gets a thumbs down is because the entire experience is an unrewarding slog.  The G.U. trilogy was released in rapid succession back in the day, and it is essentially one game split awkwardly into three parts, with some heavy padding to give each game around a 20-hour runtime.  The battles play out a bit like Star Ocean 3, but they are extremely slow and unrewarding.  The dungeons are long, repetitious, and bland, and feature encounters that are often frequent and hard to avoid.  Apart from the arena area, there are only three hub areas (one for each game).  It's very barebones.

While you can start fresh and work your way through each game, carrying your save data along the way, it is also possible to enable a cheat mode to max your character out so you can breeze through the story.  The story features a novel concept:  you play as a person who is playing a character in a fictional online game called The World.  The idea is that various problems in the game are spilling over into real life, causing users to fall into comas and so on.  It's cool, but the delivery is terrible.  Because there isn't too much of it to go around, the story is presented at a glacial pace.  What you end up getting a lot of the time is segments about how the game is more than just a game, or about how mysterious everything is.  The pacing is just awful.

It also needs to be said that the game is ridiculously cheesy even when it's trying to take itself seriously.  The characters, their lines, and a lot of what happens is hilarious or overacted to the point of absurdity.  Sometimes it's fun, but it's often as not just plain bad.    The concept is great and some of the characters were neat, but it's not enough to save the games from being terrible.

Do I recommend this game? Yes and no.
This is a "litrpg game". It is set in a massive game world, but only shows you the very narrow path of the protagonist through that. Everything is very pre-meditated and it fulfills almost all tropes of a litrpg story, but without the isekai element. 
Gameplay is solid, but only that. It is somewhat stale, and at times frustrating.
Most NPCs are very rigid, grating or overplayed. There is an undeniable charm to this, but it has to be what you are looking for.
And sure, the story moment when the character finally unlocks their new secret skills and what not is impressive, but with the game hinting at there being a choice as to what you can unlock, and the story dictating a certain path, this kinda just ended in frustration for me.

Are you okay with being shown a world that looks extremely open, but funnels you down a narrow path?
Are you okay with llusion of choice being executed badly, but still there, meaning you often think you can make a decision, but really just have to take what the game gives you?
Are you okay with NPC companions that are walking tropes with a "but" thrown in?

If you can firmly answer "Yes" to all three of these, and are looking for decently nice JRPG in a litrpg world, then I can highly recommend this game.
If even one of your answers to these questions is a "No", then I firmly advise against this game.

You have nearly no incentive to go out and grind for higher levels and better equipment, or as I like to call it: play the game.

I played .hack//Infection and the rest of the original series when I was younger, but somehow had never heard of the .hack//G.U. series until recently. So I was ecstatic when it came to Steam and I could finally give it a shot. Unfortunately, I don't think it is an improvement in any way over the original IMOQ series. 

I cannot recommend this game to anyone who hasn't already played any other .hacks and enjoyed them enough to want to continue to build upon the story and atmosphere in the .hack universe.

The combat has taken an enormous step back with it now being battles that are sectioned off and cannot be escaped without an item. Not only that, but it's almost always a group of 3 enemies, or a single "hard" enemy that gets quite repetitive.

Areas have also changed for the worse. Instead of having open fields to run in with a dungeon somewhere within each landscape, now everything has a dungeon-like layout to it that has very little variation.

Data drain is now a very tedious mini-game that you are forced to play which always, every single time throughout the entire series, starts off without a brief tutorial message. It's really disheartening to think your audience is so incapable of performing a task you've forced them into doing 30+ times by the end of the series, and still think they don't know how to attack and dodge.

A new resource has been added to the game, probably to make up for lack of grunties and hunting for grunty food called Chim Chims. These creatures serve absolutely no purpose but to make you wait to progress. In order to collect chims, there are various ways to get them, but the most common is sitting next to a switch and waiting for some to come out and flipping the switch to knock them off tracks. These are always included next to the doors that Chim Chims open, so I cannot see any purpose they serve but to inhibit progress.

This game's narrative really tasks you with suspending your disbelief pretty early on, but by the 3rd game I felt so unimmersed by how high stakes the game becomes with seemingly no reason other than to "go bigger". The story trips upon itself multiple times by the very end by plotholes and how frequently the game moves it's own goalpost.

The addition of a new episode, Reconnection (vol. 4), is the most redeeming thing about Last Recode. Its story tones it down and makes it personal again. The cutscenes use a more traditional anime style that is absolutely gorgeous. The game has a good amount of closure that vol. 3 didn't really provide in the original G.U. trilogy. 

I can really only recommend this game to anyone who played the G.U. trilogy, but not the additional episode Reconnection, even on a sale.

I can only reccomend this game to two kinds of people. If you're a fan of the original .hack series (Infection, Mutation, Outbreak, and Quarantine), you'll be able to enjoy this game as a continuation of the story, and for familiar gameplay with a few new twists. The only other group I can recommend Last Recode to is people who played the console release of the G.U. trilogy, and are looking to play the new fourth chapter. For anyone else, my criticisms follow.

First and foremost, I found this game to be buggy in a way not related to the story of rogue A.I. causing glitches in an online game. The game has, in my experience, a tendency to freeze. A lot. The game freezing has been such a constant problem across all volumes that I got in the habit of maintaining two save files just in case it decided to crash while saving and corrupt one of the files (though this has not occured at time of writing).

Secondly, the game is a bit easy. You might struggle a bit early on in Vol. 1, but it doesn't take long to get to the point where in any story areas, you're just cruising through without ever feeling threatened or challenged. It actually takes more effort to keep from getting to a point where you're high level and decked out in the best gear than it does to get there. Especially if you're carrying over data from one volume to the next - which you should be, it's the intended way to play and you miss out on some content by not doing so - you'll get to a point where with very minimal play outside of required sections, you'll never really need to worry about the story getting too tough to progress. Money ceases to be an issue vey quickly as well, as you can easily earn tons of it, and most of the time, using items isn't needed.

Third, there's some especially notable problems with Vol. 1 in particular, just in terms of story and pacing. After a short tutorial sequence, the game finishes off a brief period of story before you can get back to the action, ending in you getting sent on ANOTHER tutorial. One which largely covers the same things you just got done being taught. Further, there's an extended sequence in the story that involves entering a tournament. This is perhaps the most aggrivating element of the entire trillogy. Every single round of the tournament ends in getting kicked to a cutscene right before you could have finished the opponent off. This is not an exaggeration. It's literally every round. You NEVER get to actually win a round of the tournament. This is made worse since pretty much all of the scenes focus on your character being "outmatched" or "not ready" and getting pushed to his limits/forced to rely on his special "protagonist powers" to win in some way, shape, or form - made even worse by the fact that, as I noted earlier with the difficulty, it's not at all unreasonable that you'll have 10+ levels and better gear over your opponent and be able to end them in a single attack...if the game didn't force them to survive at 1 HP, that is. Fortunately, the games get better as they go on, but these early moments can make it hard to push through to the more engaging parts.

All the issues can be overlooked, but overall I just can't reccomend Last Recode to anyone who isn't already a fan, because without that level of investment, it's just not going to feel worth it.

First I'll say I only got so far as the end of Volume 3 and level 50 of the Forest of Pain. Since the main story is resolved and the Forest is boredom incarnate, I see no point playing this any longer.

GRAPHISMS 6/10
Mostly ok, especially during cut scenes. Quite dull and repetitive though since there are only 4 cities and 4 map layouts (5 with the Forest of Pain).

MUSIC 9/10
Excellent, though the better tracks are usually underused.

CHARACTERS 1/10
Each character is a walking cliche, the voice acting (japanese) is cringe-worthy, especially the first bad guy, who sounds like a bad disney villain.
The main character is espacially annoying during volume 1, I just wanted to reach through the screen and slap him again and again. That's how stupid and infuriating he is.

Forgetting this guy manipulated him from the start, was totally amoral, putting lots of players in coma, including the hero's girlfriend... Whatever.

IMMERSION 7/10
You navigate through the game itself, your emails, the forums, the news and a virtual card game. That works well.
However the game itself is lacking. You never see more than 5 other players on screen, even in the starting city. All the environments seem huge but empty. Quite far from the most-played MMO worldwide...

GAMEPLAY 3/10
The avatar battles are cool and refreshing.
The card game is a missed opportunity since the games are automated, so you just rely on cheesy combos to win. No skill involved.
The arena is ok at first but once you're over your opponents levels it gets boring fast. Also the main battles are scripted so you could be trashing your opponent just to lose with one cutscene.
The main battles are fun when they work, that is when you are 5 to 10 levels under your opponents. Once you're at their level, or worse way over it they become a chore... And you level realllly fast (one area gives you 2-4 levels if you're a bit under the general level) so you'll hit max level very quickly.
The weapon change is mostly pointless, adapting your weapon to your ennemy is useless since the differences are not that huge AND you'll be crushing them anyway. You'll also be punished for switching weapons too much since your proficiency won't rise. 
The guns are cool though.

STORY 1/10
The story is full of plot holes (like the main character somehow forgetting all he knew about the game once he goes back to level 1), the ending (as of volume 3) is totally unsatisfying.
The plot itself is boring and predictable: bad guy causes bad AI to threaten the game world, the whole internet and the real world. Good guys trash him, crush the AI. Rinse and repeat.
Too bad, because the main idea (influence of the virtual world over the real world) is brilliant and was quite original at the time.

This is not a good game. I remember having fun playing the trilogy 10 years ago on my PS2, but I guess I just had more tolerance and patience for these types of games. That being said, I remember that even back then I found the game far from perfect and somewhat boring, but now I find it extremely boring.

The biggest problem is the pacing of the game. The gameplay is constantly interrupted for the sake of the plot. Usually, I don't mind that. I'm not the type of guy who hates story-driven games. I do mind it in this game, though, because the plot is served to you in a form of long, badly written dialogues in which characters just stand still and only camera angles change. Every one does that 10-second pause after each sentence. No one is straight forward about anything. They say something cryptic, wait for someone else to ask about details and then go into them. If that wasn't enough, sometimes one of the characters ends up saying a simplified version of what the other one said, making the first half of the dialogue completely pointless.
Example:
-We are Epitaph Users.
...10 seconds later...
-Epitaph Users?
...10 seconds later...
-Yes, that means we...(starts blabbing for 3 minutes)
...10 seconds later...
-Oh, so you are basically this and this?
...10 seconds later...
-You can put it that way.
Couldn't the character say only the simplified version?
Also, there are these long exchanges that lead nowhere.
Example:
-Haseo!
...10 seconds later...
-What?
...10 seconds later...
-You have to save him!
...10 seconds later...
-Why me?
...10 seconds later...
-Because he said to contact you!
...10 seconds later...
-Me?
...10 seconds later...
-Mhm.
90% of the dialogue is structured like that and most of the game is dialogue. I played it for over 20 hours and I feel like 15 of them was spent on it. I know you can skip it, but I do want to know what is going on in the game and that is the only way to find out. The game takes place in an MMO and in order to progress in story you often have to log out in order to read an email and log back in. Sometimes you have to log out, read an email, log back in just to have a dialogue with a character, get another email, log out again, read the new one and log back in. It seriously seems like the devs went out of their way just to make the game boring. There is even a quest that you have to do in order to progress in the game in which you have to walk up to multiple NPCs scattered around the hub world just to listen to them talk. After the quest is done your character makes a comment on how boring it was almost as if the devs were aware of it. If you acknowledge that something is boring maybe you should fix it or get rid of it completely.

Story isn't that great either. Like I said before, the game is happening in a game, which in my opinion isn't a very good setting for a story-driven game. Everything ends up being less powerful and less meaningful since it all happens in some silly MMO. There is a character who gives people lectures about morality and treating others well, but since it is just a player in a video game, it is hard to take him seriously. He's just some guy who gets back home after work, puts on his VR headset and gets too much into the game. There is a scene early in the game that shows a character being killed. It's meant to be dramatic but you get pulled out of it with a line like ‘I love PKing those noobs. LOL’. You quickly realize that it's not a person being killed. It's just a character in a video game being PKed. Every battle that is meant to be spectacular is also diminished when you are aware that the ones who fight in it aren't meant to be people, but some 3D models controlled by a bunch of teens who scream stuff like ‘BONE CRUSHER!’ and wake up their moms downstairs. That makes the story very unreliable since people end up being hurt in real life through the game, but no one thinks of logging out or taking off their headset or turning off their PC whenever something like that happens. There are news about people ending up in a coma from playing the game all over the internet but nobody cares. People still log into it; mothers still let their kids play it. The relations between characters aren't very credible either. There means to be some kind of romance between some of the characters, but again, it's a video game. These people go grinding together a couple times and fall in love with each other without ever speaking with each other or seeing each other in real life. If that wasn't enough, the protagonist is often mean to his comrades to the point they cry (about someone being mean to them in a video game) as if he was meant to realize that he's unnecessarily rude, swallow his pride and apologize, but that never happens. His ‘friends’ eventually come back to him and they end up apologizing instead.

I can't really say anything bad about sound and visuals. The game looks nice till this day. The character designs are fun, memorable and fit the MMO setting. The same goes for the music.

There isn't much to the gameplay, but it is fun. Like I said, visuals and sound are nice. The battle theme gets you pumped up and the particle effects and sound effects make it satisfying to hit enemies. It is kind of repetitive, but as you progress through the game your character learns to wield different types of weapon so it isn't that bad. Also, each weapon has it's own visual design and their attacks varies a little, even between the ones of the same type. Unfortunately, the combat is pretty easy. You can tackle enemies that are 8 levels above you and gain levels very quickly. You collect healing items to help you during longer adventures and there's also a mechanic that lets you slowly regain health when you stand still. Both of these things are completely useless in this remaster. They added a new mechanic. When you lose a fight you can press ‘retry’ and you begin the fight that you just lost at with full HP and SP. There is no punishment for losing. If anything, you are REWARDED with full HP and SP for losing. Why would you ever use healing items or stand still for few minutes when you are dying, when you can just rush into a battle, get yourself killed, press ‘retry’ and regain your HP and SP for free? That being said, going to various areas to beat up monsters and collect new loot is the best part of the game, so I have no idea why they do everything to stop you from doing that. Of course you can go grinding whenever you want, but you will quickly become too OP for the story quests which will make them even more boring.

I didn't have any technical problems with the game. I see people posting about crashes, freezes and corrupted save files. I never experienced any of these. Either I'm lucky or the game got a proper update.

I never made it to the new content and I probably never will, but I saw the trailer on steam and I'll say this; for god's sake stop intentionally rendering CG cutscenes at low framerates. It looks awful. It looks especially bad in this since previous cutscenes form PS2 era run at smooth 60FPS. They seriously added choppy 5FPS cutscenes that look worse than the original ones form 11 years ago to this remaster.

Overall, if I had to describe .hack//G.U. Last Recode with one word it would be ‘boring’. The gameplay, visuals and music are ok, but in the long run you won't enjoy this game due to it's focus on mediocre story explained in form of badly written dialogue. I cannot recommend it to anyone. Not even nostalgic fans of the series.

OK, how do I even start? I was thinking about some good points to start with, but... there are none. I've only played to Vol 3, as it has a proper ending for whatever story they tried to make, and I have to assume that Vol 4 just adds more of that boring crap.

OK, three volumes. They are all (mostly) the same game, down to the same collection "quests" and how you progress the main story by doing arena fights. Oh, except for vol 3 which ends the initial story eventually... and then just pulls a new even bigger baddie out of the hat. Although this time around, they just beat it up somewhat quickly, because they don't have another three volumes.

And while the game claims to be set in a MMO, which it is, they completely failed to actually create that game. The dungeons are utterly boring and repetitive, and there's no story for the players to follow.  I can't see why anyone would ever want to play the MMO.

But, for some reason, whenever a character wants to tell me something about the "real" story, they make me go through these boring dungeons and only tell me at the end for some reason. Either that, or they send me an "EMail". Which, btw, is what drives most of the story -- NPCs telling me something they do or don't know or assume, or NPCs telling me something they found out. My job is to go through the never-changing dungeons and hear what NPCs tell me.

Oh, did I mention that the game is about certain players with ingame superpowers of some sort that nobody else is supposed to know about? Yet, the game doesn't mind if I put characters that aren't supposed to know anything into my party when going to those meetings or doing stuff they aren't supposed to know about. The game just feels randomly mixed together. In volume 2, you're even suddenly getting messages from another person you've never heard about that's supposed to be dead, leading you to special weapons... again, no explanations and no context.

The characters are often annoying, starting with the protagonist himself whining about a character that we've never met being unconscious in the real world due to the weird stuff going on in the game. Which is a bit of stretch, but whatever. Unfortunately, the story never actually develops in any way and just drags on and on and on, until vol 3 deus-ex-machinas it to an end.
Other characters are often annoying as well, especially Endrance, but we're in 2020 so I'm not allowed to go into specifics.

And then there are the Avatar battles. These have no levels, no gear, no skills, no items, nothing. They are a lot like QTEs, as attacks have one specific way to avoid them.

Feel free to play it if you really want to; I just don't see any reason to recommend this to anyone.

Still, it's quite playable now, if you want to revisit old times.

Then there's volume 4.  It's a shame, since this was likely somebody's passion project, but the only words that come to mind here are "cut corners".  When it comes to gameplay, that might be a good thing, depending on your point of view, since playing to "complete" status took me less than 7 hours playtime (as compared to over 20 hours for the prior volumes), but that was accomplished by locking down practically every non-essential item both inside the game and on the "desktop" you launch the game from, all justified story-wise by The World preparing to shut down.  On top of that, the animation quality in cutscenes changed significantly... oh, the images being animated are arguably better, but the animation itself isn't as smooth as it was in prior volumes.  Worst of all, in my opinion, the new story doesn't really hold up, compared to prior volumes.

Long story short, if you're eager to play/revisit the original volumes for a little nostalgia, by all means go ahead.  But, if you're looking for a new RPG to play, or you're looking to continue a story you liked from decades ago, just let it go.

Okay, I know how this looks but its not what you think... I mean, why would I play all four games of the story to completion if I hated it? I just have very mixed feelings regarding the .hack//G.U. games that I thought needed to be expressed to people interested in JRPGs and don't know what they're getting into. The short version is that I like the combat, but everything else in this game is a mixed bag - including the story.

Let me start with the first game. This one was a doozy and not in a good way. You play through the prologue, which is supposed to set up the plot and character arcs going forward only for a massive time jump to be placed right afterwards and skip an enormous amount of story and character development to the point that the main character is practically a completely different character than the one the story sells you on in the prologue... let alone the fact that the main character now has a goal that came out of nowhere and has no emotional weight behind it due to the fact that the game chose to pull all of this super edge lord shit out of its arse out of nowhere. I mean, if they wanted to start the story there, the prologue should've been adjusted to introduce the player to this character motivation and plot. AND YES, I'm well aware that there's an anime that tells the story of this missing period of time but the game suffers so much due to the fact that this information and story isn't apart of the actual game. Though there were excellent emotional moments scattered throughout the latter part of the game, the first hack GU game is mediocre from a story telling perspective at best and lazy at worst. Also certain dungeons along with the arena battles all run like trash at like 0.1 miles per hour.
The second game has more great emotional moments than the first with more likeable characters working through the stereotypical anime plot, but the plot and dialogue aren't anything to write home about and made me laugh when they weren't supposed to. Also this second game introduced the dreaded warp levels that slow down the game to a snail's pace, which added to the addition of more arena battles and more visits to the same dungeons over and over made for a slog as I constantly tried to keep myself motivated with the combat, the side quests and the next plot development.
There are more warp levels in the third game and it goes hard on the emotional elements while still remaining just as copy-paste anime in the rest of the story. It literally gets so anime that the last boss battle was won through the power of friendship... I am not joking. However, the colourful band of characters and plot twists did keep me constantly invested in the game, so not all bad... but most of the levels in the third game run at the speed of a fat guy on a moped. On the other hand, the outer dungeons were a nice addition to the dungeon variation of this game as well as the tower-style dungeons... but that's the only additional new dungeons and I'm not joking because you'll even get tired of those dungeons by the end of this game. Sorry for the glimmer of hope.
The fourth game was shorter. That made it much more palatable than the other games and it had more very well animated CG cutscenes. The dungeons repeat so much that it makes you go mad, like it is legit the exact same dungeons that you've played through over and over again in the past three games. The only thing I can praise this game for is that you only have to enter three dungeons before the final battle, which keeps it short and sweet... if not for each of the three dungeons having multiple floors that you have to slog through. I know it sound like I'm moaning, but do remember that I'd been seeing these same repeating hallways for almost a hundred hours at this point. I think anyone would go mad at this point. Also, this final game goes hard on the stereotypical anime moments, like there's no explanation for the final battle with in-game logic... it's just the power of friendship again. THE POWER OF F*CKING FRIENDSHIP! 

If you can stomach all of the complaints I have for the .hack//G.U. games, then go ahead... but if even one of these things are nitpicks you can't stomach, then don't waste your time and money. 



P.S. If the developers ever decide to make another set of games in the hack universe like the end of the fourth game hints at, then I hope to GOD that they make these games, for one, much better written without needing to rely on stereotypical anime moments. Two, that the exploration is much more expansive and varied (either have an complex and multifaceted open world or take a page from DmC in level design). Three, that the game will look like it was made for modern platforms at least instead of looking like it's all from the early PS2 era. Four, that the gameplay won't feel so bloody repetitive. And finally, that they might actually include the real world events into the story (this comes from the fact that I saw loads of interesting news articles in these games that looked like so much more fun to play than the world, and that there's so much off-screen character development that happens with these characters while they're away from the game. Both of these points just seemed like a huge missed opportunity).

There, I've said my peace.
